## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
Prove universal inequality
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m} < 2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}
\]
for \(m>n\ge\max(A)\), and identify sharpness mechanism.

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Show a monotone-density-doubling lemma for sets of multiples:
for \(B=\bigcup_{a\in A} a\mathbb N\), density profile \(D(x)=|B\cap[1,x]|/x\) satisfies
\[
\sup_{m>n}\frac{D(m)}{D(n)}\le 2-\eta(n,A),
\]
with \(\eta\ge0\) and \(\eta\to0\) only for near-singleton extremizers.

### B. Proven Lemmas (this note)

#### Lemma B1 (inclusion-exclusion form)
\[
|B\cap[1,x]|=\sum_{\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A}(-1)^{|S|+1}\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\operatorname{lcm}(S)}\right\rfloor.
\]

**Proof.**
Standard inclusion-exclusion over divisibility by elements of \(A\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (density approximation)
\[
D(x)=\sum_{\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A}\frac{(-1)^{|S|+1}}{\operatorname{lcm}(S)}+O_A(1/x).
\]

**Proof.**
Replace floors in B1 by real parts plus \(O(1)\), then divide by \(x\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (Singleton Case Is True)
For \(A=\{a\}\), \(a\ge2\), and any \(m>n\ge a\),
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n},
\quad
B=a\mathbb N.
\]

**Proof.**
Here
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,x]|}{x}=\frac{\lfloor x/a\rfloor}{x}.
\]
Set \(u=\lfloor n/a\rfloor\ge1\). Then:
1. \(\lfloor m/a\rfloor/m\le 1/a\).
2. \(n<a(u+1)\), hence
\[
2\frac{\lfloor n/a\rfloor}{n}

=2\frac{u}{n}
>
2\frac{u}{a(u+1)}.
\]
If \(u\ge2\), then \(2u/(u+1)>1\), so RHS \(>1/a\), proving strict inequality.
If \(u=1\), then \(n\in[a,2a-1]\), so
\[
2\frac{\lfloor n/a\rfloor}{n}=2/n\ge 2/(2a-1)>1/a\ge \lfloor m/a\rfloor/m.
\]
Thus inequality holds in all cases. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B4 (Sharpness Constant 2 From Singleton Family)
For \(A=\{a\}\), choosing \(n=2a-1\), \(m=2a\),
\[
\frac{ \frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m} }{ \frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n} }
=\frac{(1/a)}{(1/(2a-1))}
=2-\frac1a\to2.
\]

**Proof.**
\(|B\cap[1,2a]|=2\), \(|B\cap[1,2a-1]|=1\). Substitute directly. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B5 (Eventual-In-\(n\) Inequality For Fixed \(A\))
Let \(A\) be fixed, \(k=|A|\), \(C_A:=2^k-1\), \(a_{\max}:=\max(A)\), and
\[
\delta_A=\sum_{\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A}\frac{(-1)^{|S|+1}}{\mathrm{lcm}(S)}.
\]
Then for all
\[
n\ge \max\{a_{\max},\,3C_A/\delta_A\},
\]
and all \(m>n\),
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
From inclusion-exclusion,
\[
M_A(x):=|B\cap[1,x]|=\delta_A x + E_A(x),
\]
where each floor contributes an error in \((-1,0]\), hence
\[
|E_A(x)|\le C_A.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}\le \delta_A+\frac{C_A}{m}\le \delta_A+\frac{C_A}{n},
\]
and
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}\ge \delta_A-\frac{C_A}{n}.
\]
So it suffices to show
\[
\delta_A+\frac{C_A}{n}<2\left(\delta_A-\frac{C_A}{n}\right),
\]
equivalent to \(\delta_A>3C_A/n\), i.e. \(n>3C_A/\delta_A\). The stated threshold gives strict inequality. \(\square\)

#### Corollary B6 (Finite-Range Reduction)
For each fixed finite \(A\), EP-488 reduces to checking finitely many \(n\), namely
\[
\max(A)\le n<3C_A/\delta_A,
\]
since all larger \(n\) are covered by Lemma B5.

**Proof.**
Immediate from Lemma B5. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B7 (Exact sparse-edge case \(B(n)=|A|\))
Let \(A\subset \{2,\dots,n\}\) be finite and
\[
B=\bigcup_{a\in A} a\mathbb N,\qquad |B\cap[1,n]|=|A|=:k.
\]
Then for every \(m>n\),
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
The condition \(|B\cap[1,n]|=|A|\) means that, up to \(n\), each \(a\in A\) contributes only its first multiple.
Hence \(2a>n\) for all \(a\in A\), i.e. \(a>n/2\).
Now for \(m>n\),
\[
|B\cap[1,m]|
\le \sum_{a\in A}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{a}\right\rfloor
< \sum_{a\in A}\frac{m}{a}
< \sum_{a\in A}\frac{2m}{n}
=\frac{2km}{n}.
\]
Divide by \(m\), and use \(|B\cap[1,n]|=k\):
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{2k}{n}
=2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]
\(\square\)

#### Lemma B8 (Near-extremal structure at small denominator)
If \(n\ge\max(A)\) and \(|B\cap[1,n]|=1\), then \(A=\{a\}\) and \(n\in[a,2a-1]\), so EP-488 follows from Lemma B3.

**Proof.**
Since \(n\ge\max(A)\), every \(a\in A\) lies in \([1,n]\cap B\). Thus \(|A|\le |B\cap[1,n]|=1\), so \(A=\{a\}\).
Also \(|B\cap[1,n]|=\lfloor n/a\rfloor=1\), equivalent to \(a\le n\le 2a-1\).
Apply Lemma B3. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B9 (Case \(|B\cap[1,n]|=2\) is fully resolved)
If \(n\ge\max(A)\), \(|B\cap[1,n]|=2\), and \(m>n\), then
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Write \(t:=|B\cap[1,n]|=2\).
Since each \(a\in A\) belongs to \(B\cap[1,n]\), we have \(|A|\le2\).

If \(|A|=1\), this is the singleton case (Lemma B3), done.

If \(|A|=2\), say \(A=\{a,b\}\), then \(B\cap[1,n]\) has only the two base elements \(a,b\), so there is no second multiple of either within \([1,n]\). Thus \(n<2a\) and \(n<2b\), equivalently \(a,b>n/2\). Therefore
\[
|B\cap[1,m]|
\le \left\lfloor\frac{m}{a}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{b}\right\rfloor
< \frac{m}{a}+\frac{m}{b}
< \frac{2m}{n}+\frac{2m}{n}
=\frac{4m}{n}.
\]
Divide by \(m\):
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{4}{n}
=2\cdot\frac{2}{n}
=2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]
\(\square\)

#### Lemma B10 (Case \(|B\cap[1,n]|=3\) is fully resolved)
If \(n\ge\max(A)\), \(|B\cap[1,n]|=3\), and \(m>n\), then
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}
=\frac{6}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Set \(t:=|B\cap[1,n]|=3\). Since each \(a\in A\) lies in \(B\cap[1,n]\), \(|A|\le3\).

If \(|A|=1\), apply Lemma B3.

If \(|A|=3\), then \(|B\cap[1,n]|=|A|\), so apply Lemma B7.

It remains \(|A|=2\), say \(A=\{a,b\}\) with \(a<b\). Then
\[
|B\cap[1,m]|
\le \left\lfloor\frac{m}{a}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{b}\right\rfloor
< \frac{m}{a}+\frac{m}{b},
\]
so it is enough to show
\[
\frac1a+\frac1b<\frac6n.
\]
Write \(u:=\lfloor n/a\rfloor\in\{1,2,3\}\), since \(u\ge1\) (as \(a\le n\)) and \(u\le3\) (otherwise \(a,2a,3a,4a\le n\) would already force at least 4 elements of \(B\cap[1,n]\)).

Case \(u=1\): then \(a>n/2\), hence \(1/a<2/n\). Also \(b>a>n/2\), so \(1/b<2/n\). Therefore \(1/a+1/b<4/n<6/n\).

Case \(u=2\): then \(a>n/3\), so \(1/a<3/n\). Also \(b>a>n/3\), so \(1/b<3/n\). Hence \(1/a+1/b<6/n\).

Case \(u=3\): multiples of \(a\) up to \(n\) are \(\{a,2a,3a\}\). Since \(|B\cap[1,n]|=3\), every multiple of \(b\) up to \(n\) must lie in \(\{a,2a,3a\}\). In particular \(b\in\{2a,3a\}\), so \(b\ge2a\). Now \(a>n/4\) (from \(u=3\)), thus \(1/a<4/n\), and \(b\ge2a>n/2\), so \(1/b<2/n\). Therefore \(1/a+1/b<6/n\).

In all cases, \(|B\cap[1,m]|/m<6/n=2|B\cap[1,n]|/n\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B11 (Divisibility reduction)
Let \(A\) be finite and
\[
B=\bigcup_{a\in A} a\mathbb N.
\]
If \(a_1,a_2\in A\) with \(a_1\mid a_2\), then removing \(a_2\) does not change \(B\).
Hence there is a reduced set \(A_{\min}\subseteq A\) (no two elements divide each other) with
\[
\bigcup_{a\in A_{\min}} a\mathbb N = B.
\]

**Proof.**
If \(a_1\mid a_2\), then \(a_2\mathbb N\subseteq a_1\mathbb N\), so \(a_2\) is redundant in the union. Repeating finitely many times yields \(A_{\min}\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B12 (Case \(|B\cap[1,n]|=4\) is fully resolved)
If \(n\ge\max(A)\), \(|B\cap[1,n]|=4\), and \(m>n\), then
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}
=\frac{8}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Replace \(A\) by the reduced generator set \(G:=A_{\min}\) from Lemma B11; this does not change \(B\). Let \(r:=|G|\). Since every \(g\in G\) belongs to \(B\cap[1,n]\), we have \(1\le r\le4\).

If \(r=1\), apply Lemma B3.

If \(r=4\), then \(|B\cap[1,n]|=|G|\), so apply Lemma B7.

It remains \(r=2\) or \(r=3\). Write \(G=\{g_1<\cdots<g_r\}\), and \(u_i:=\lfloor n/g_i\rfloor\).

For any \(i\), \(u_i\le4\), otherwise \(g_i,2g_i,3g_i,4g_i,5g_i\le n\) would already give at least 5 points in \(B\cap[1,n]\), contradiction.

**Case \(r=2\).**
Suppose \(u_1=4\). Then \(g_1,2g_1,3g_1,4g_1\in B\cap[1,n]\). Since \(G\) is reduced, \(g_2\) is not a multiple of \(g_1\), so \(g_2\notin\{g_1,2g_1,3g_1,4g_1\}\), forcing at least 5 points in \(B\cap[1,n]\), contradiction. Hence \(u_1\le3\), so \(g_1>n/4\). Also \(g_2>g_1>n/4\). Therefore
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}
\le \frac{\lfloor m/g_1\rfloor+\lfloor m/g_2\rfloor}{m}
< \frac1{g_1}+\frac1{g_2}
< \frac4n+\frac4n
=\frac8n.
\]

**Case \(r=3\).**
Claim: at most one \(u_i\) equals 2. Indeed, if \(u_i=u_j=2\) with \(i\ne j\), then \(2g_i,2g_j\le n\) are two distinct extra points beyond the three base points \(g_1,g_2,g_3\), so \(|B\cap[1,n]|\ge5\), contradiction.
Also no \(u_i\ge3\): if \(u_i\ge3\), then \(2g_i,3g_i\le n\) give two distinct extra points beyond the three bases, again contradiction.
Thus one has either:
- all \(u_i=1\), hence each \(g_i>n/2\); or
- exactly one \(u_i=2\) and the other two are 1, hence one generator \(>n/3\) and two \(>n/2\).
In both subcases,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^3 \frac1{g_i}
< \frac3n+\frac2n+\frac2n
=\frac7n
<\frac8n.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}
\le \sum_{i=1}^3 \frac{\lfloor m/g_i\rfloor}{m}
< \sum_{i=1}^3 \frac1{g_i}
<\frac8n.
\]

All cases give \(|B\cap[1,m]|/m<8/n=2|B\cap[1,n]|/n\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B13 (All reduced two-generator sets are fully resolved)
Let \(G=\{a,b\}\) with \(2\le a<b\), \(a\nmid b\), and
\[
B=a\mathbb N\cup b\mathbb N.
\]
Then for every \(n\ge b\) and every \(m>n\),
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Set
\[
u:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{a}\Big\rfloor,\quad
v:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{b}\Big\rfloor,\quad
w:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{\mathrm{lcm}(a,b)}\Big\rfloor.
\]
Then
\[
|B\cap[1,n]|=u+v-w.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}
\le \frac{\lfloor m/a\rfloor+\lfloor m/b\rfloor}{m}
<\frac1a+\frac1b.
\]
Now \(u\le n/a<u+1\), \(v\le n/b<v+1\), hence
\[
\frac1a+\frac1b<\frac{u+1}{n}+\frac{v+1}{n}=\frac{u+v+2}{n}.
\]
So it is enough to show
\[
u+v+2\le 2(u+v-w),
\]
equivalently
\[
2\le u+v-2w. \tag{*}
\]

Because \(a\nmid b\), with \(g=\gcd(a,b)\) we have \(a/g\ge2\), so
\[
\mathrm{lcm}(a,b)=\frac{ab}{g}=b\frac{a}{g}\ge 2b.
\]
Therefore
\[
w\le \Big\lfloor\frac{n}{2b}\Big\rfloor\le \Big\lfloor\frac{v}{2}\Big\rfloor.
\]
Hence
\[
u+v-2w\ge u+v-2\Big\lfloor\frac v2\Big\rfloor \in\{u,u+1\}.
\]
If \(u\ge2\), this is at least 2. If \(u=1\), then \(n<2a<2b\), so \(v=1\), and then
\[
u+v-2w\ge 1+1-2\lfloor 1/2\rfloor=2.
\]
Thus \((*)\) always holds. Consequently
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{u+v+2}{n}\le \frac{2(u+v-w)}{n}
=2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]
\(\square\)

#### Lemma B14 (Case \(|B\cap[1,n]|=5\) is fully resolved)
If \(n\ge\max(A)\), \(|B\cap[1,n]|=5\), and \(m>n\), then
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}
=\frac{10}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Replace \(A\) by reduced generators \(G=A_{\min}\) (Lemma B11), and let \(r:=|G|\). Since each \(g\in G\) lies in \(B\cap[1,n]\), \(1\le r\le5\).

If \(r=1\), use Lemma B3.  
If \(r=2\), use Lemma B13.  
If \(r=5\), then \(|B\cap[1,n]|=|G|\), so use Lemma B7.

It remains \(r=3\) or \(r=4\). Write \(G=\{g_1<\cdots<g_r\}\), and \(u_i:=\lfloor n/g_i\rfloor\).
As before,
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}
\le \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{\lfloor m/g_i\rfloor}{m}
< \sum_{i=1}^r \frac1{g_i}
< \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{u_i+1}{n}
=\frac{(\sum_i u_i)+r}{n}.
\]
So it is enough to prove
\[
\sum_i u_i \le 10-r. \tag{*}
\]

Subcase \(r=3\): need \(\sum u_i\le7\).

- \(u_1\le3\): if \(u_1\ge4\), then \(g_1,2g_1,3g_1,4g_1\in B\cap[1,n]\), and \(g_2,g_3\) are distinct non-multiples of \(g_1\), hence outside this 4-set; so \(|B\cap[1,n]|\ge6\), contradiction.
- \(u_2\le2\): if \(u_2\ge3\), then the sets \(\{g_1,2g_1,3g_1\}\) and \(\{g_2,2g_2,3g_2\}\) have intersection size at most 1, so their union has at least 5 points. Also \(g_3\) is not divisible by \(g_1\) or \(g_2\), hence is outside that union, forcing at least 6 points, contradiction.

Thus \(u_1\le3\), \(u_2\le2\), \(u_3\le u_2\le2\), so \(\sum u_i\le3+2+2=7\), proving \((*)\). Hence
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{7+3}{n}=\frac{10}{n}.
\]

Subcase \(r=4\): need \(\sum u_i\le6\).

- \(u_1\le2\): if \(u_1\ge3\), then \(g_1,2g_1,3g_1\) plus \(g_2,g_3,g_4\) (all outside \(g_1\mathbb N\) by reducedness) give at least 6 points, contradiction.
- At most one \(u_i\) equals 2: if \(u_i=u_j=2\) with \(i\neq j\), then \(g_i,2g_i,g_j,2g_j\) are at least 4 distinct points (equalities like \(2g_i=g_j\) are forbidden by reducedness), and adding the two other generators gives at least 6 points, contradiction.

So \(\sum u_i\le2+1+1+1=5\), stronger than \((*)\), and
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{5+4}{n}=\frac{9}{n}<\frac{10}{n}.
\]

All cases yield the target inequality. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B15 (Case \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6\): resolved for reduced size \(r=4,5\))
Let \(n\ge\max(A)\), \(m>n\), \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6\), and let \(G=A_{\min}\) be the reduced generator set (Lemma B11), with \(r:=|G|\).
If \(r\in\{4,5\}\), then
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}=\frac{12}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Write \(G=\{g_1<\cdots<g_r\}\), \(u_i:=\lfloor n/g_i\rfloor\). As in earlier lemmas,
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}
\le \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{\lfloor m/g_i\rfloor}{m}
< \sum_{i=1}^r \frac1{g_i}
< \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{u_i+1}{n}
=\frac{(\sum_i u_i)+r}{n}.
\]
So it suffices to bound \(\sum_i u_i\).

Let \(E:=|B\cap[1,n]|-r=6-r\), the number of non-base points in \(B\cap[1,n]\).

For each \(i\) with \(u_i\ge2\), the point \(2g_i\le n\) is a non-base point. These \(2g_i\) are pairwise distinct, so
\[
s:=\#\{i:u_i\ge2\}\le E. \tag{1}
\]
Also, if some \(u_i\ge4\), then \(2g_i,3g_i,4g_i\) are three distinct non-base points, forcing \(E\ge3\), impossible for \(r=4,5\). Hence
\[
u_i\le3\quad\text{for all }i. \tag{2}
\]

Case \(r=5\): then \(E=1\). By (1), \(s\le1\). Since \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6>5=r\), we must have \(s=1\). By (2), the unique index with \(u_i\ge2\) has \(u_i\in\{2,3\}\); but \(u_i=3\) would already give two non-base points \(2g_i,3g_i\), contradicting \(E=1\). So that index has \(u_i=2\), and all others have \(u_i=1\). Therefore
\[
\sum_i u_i=2+1+1+1+1=6.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{6+5}{n}=\frac{11}{n}<\frac{12}{n}.
\]

Case \(r=4\): then \(E=2\). By (1), \(s\le2\), and since \(6>4\), we have \(s\ge1\).

- If \(s=1\), then one \(u_i\in\{2,3\}\), others are 1, so \(\sum_i u_i\le3+1+1+1=6\).
- If \(s=2\), then two indices have \(u\in\{2,3\}\), others are 1. They cannot both be 3, because then the two progressions contribute non-base points \(\{2g_i,3g_i\}\) and \(\{2g_j,3g_j\}\), which contain at least three distinct numbers (since \(2g_i\neq2g_j\), and both \(3g_i,3g_j\) cannot simultaneously coincide with \(\{2g_i,2g_j\}\)); this would force \(E\ge3\), contradiction. So the pair is at most \((3,2)\), and
\[
\sum_i u_i\le3+2+1+1=7.
\]

Thus in both subcases, \(\sum_i u_i\le7\), and
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{7+4}{n}=\frac{11}{n}<\frac{12}{n}.
\]

Therefore the claim holds for \(r=4,5\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B21 (Case \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6\): resolved for reduced size \(r=3\))
Let \(n\ge\max(A)\), \(m>n\), \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6\), and let \(G=A_{\min}=\{a<b<c\}\) (Lemma B11).  
Then
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}=\frac{12}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
Set
\[
u_1:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{a}\Big\rfloor,\quad
u_2:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{b}\Big\rfloor,\quad
u_3:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{c}\Big\rfloor.
\]
As usual,
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}
\le \sum_{g\in G}\frac{\lfloor m/g\rfloor}{m}
< \sum_{g\in G}\frac1g
< \frac{u_1+u_2+u_3+3}{n}. \tag{1}
\]
So it suffices to prove \(u_1+u_2+u_3\le8\).

First, \(u_1\le4\): if \(u_1\ge5\), then \(a,2a,3a,4a,5a\le n\), giving at least 5 points from \(a\mathbb N\) in \([1,n]\), plus \(b\) and \(c\) (not multiples of \(a\), by reducedness), hence at least 7 points in \(B\cap[1,n]\), contradiction.

Now claim \(u_2\le2\). Suppose \(u_2\ge3\). Then \(u_1\ge u_2\ge3\), so
\[
2a,3a\le n,\qquad 2b,3b\le n.
\]
Since \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6\) and we already have 3 base points \(a,b,c\), there are exactly 3 non-base points total. Therefore the four numbers \(2a,3a,2b,3b\) cannot be all distinct; at least one equality must hold between one of \(\{2a,3a\}\) and one of \(\{2b,3b\}\).
The only possible equality is
\[
3a=2b,
\]
because \(2a=2b\), \(3a=3b\) force \(a=b\), and \(2a=3b\) gives \(b< a\), impossible.
Hence \(b=\frac{3a}{2}\), so \(u_2\ge3\) implies
\[
n\ge 3b=\frac{9a}{2},
\]
thus \(u_1=\lfloor n/a\rfloor\ge4\), so \(4a\le n\).
Now
\[
2a,\ 3a(=2b),\ 4a,\ 3b\le n
\]
are four distinct non-base points (indeed \(3b=\frac{9a}{2}\neq 2a,3a,4a\)). This contradicts that only 3 non-base points exist. Therefore \(u_2\le2\).

Since \(u_3\le u_2\), we get
\[
u_1+u_2+u_3\le 4+2+2=8.
\]
Applying (1):
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<\frac{8+3}{n}=\frac{11}{n}<\frac{12}{n}.
\]
So the target inequality holds. \(\square\)

### Failed shortcut (now explicit)

The tempting bound
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}\le \frac{|B\cap[1,n]|+1}{n}\qquad(m>n)
\]
is false in general.
Concrete counterexample (found in standalone check):
\[
A=\{3,4,22,38,46,54,65\},\quad n=74,\quad m=81,
\]
for which
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}=\frac{45}{81}\approx 0.55556
>
\frac{40+1}{74}=\frac{41}{74}\approx 0.55405.
\]
So this route cannot close the problem.

### C. Main unresolved point

The remaining gap is now sharply localized:

- By Lemmas B3/B8/B9/B10/B12/B14, all cases with \(|B\cap[1,n]|\le5\) are done.
- By Lemma B13 (plus divisibility reduction, Lemma B11), all problems with reduced generator size \(\le2\) are done for all \(n\).
- By Lemmas B15 and B21, the full \(|B\cap[1,n]|=6\) layer is done (all reduced sizes \(r\le6\)).
- By Lemma B5, all sufficiently large \(n\) (for fixed \(A\)) are done.

So the unsolved core is the finite-window regime with
\[
7\le |B\cap[1,n]|<\infty
\]
and reduced generator size \(\ge3\), below the explicit B5 threshold.

### D. General Techniques (to finish full EP-488)

The layer-by-layer closure is useful but likely not sufficient by itself for a full theorem. The global routes are:

1. Sieve-weight majorant with sharp finite-\(n\) error:
\[
M_A(x)=\delta_A x+E_A(x),\qquad E_A(x)=\sum_{\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A}(-1)^{|S|+1}\Bigl(\Big\lfloor\frac{x}{\mathrm{lcm}(S)}\Big\rfloor-\frac{x}{\mathrm{lcm}(S)}\Bigr).
\]
Need a sign-sensitive bound on \(E_A(m)-2E_A(n)\), not just \(|E_A|\le C_A\).

2. Extremal reduction to minimal antichains:
after Lemma B11, reduce to \(A_{\min}\) and prove a universal extremal principle:
near-equality in the factor \(2\) inequality forces singleton-like structure.
This is a stability theorem, analogous to Tao-style near-extremizer rigidity.

3. LP/duality formulation:
for fixed \(n\), maximize
\[
\sup_{m>n}\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|/m}{|B\cap[1,n]|/n}
\]
over reduced multiplicative set-systems.
If dual certificate gives value \(<2\), full theorem follows.

4. Finite-window compactness:
combine B5 with a structural bound showing that for fixed \(t:=|B\cap[1,n]|\), only finitely many reduced patterns of first-hit multiplicities \((u_i)\) are extremal; then solve each pattern class symbolically.

### E. Concrete Missing Lemmas (Global)

- **GL1 (signed discrepancy transport):**
  prove \(E_A(m)\le 2E_A(n)+\Theta_A(n,m)\) with \(\Theta_A\) summably small/uniformly negative in the critical window.
- **GL2 (near-extremizer rigidity):**
  if
  \[
  \frac{|B\cap[1,m]|/m}{|B\cap[1,n]|/n}>2-\varepsilon,
  \]
  then \(A_{\min}\) has a dominant generator \(a_*\) and all others contribute \(O_\varepsilon(1/n)\) to density.
- **GL3 (pattern finiteness at fixed \(t\)):**
  for fixed \(t\), reduced \(A\) with \(|B\cap[1,n]|=t\) has bounded admissible profile complexity (independent of arithmetic size of elements), enabling full symbolic elimination.

### F. GL1 Progress: Signed Discrepancy Transport (executed)

We now make GL1 explicit in a weighted-lcm basis.

For fixed finite \(A\), let \(\mathcal L(A)\) be the set of distinct lcm-values
\[
\mathcal L(A):=\{\operatorname{lcm}(S):\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A\},
\]
and define coefficients
\[
\lambda_d:=\sum_{\substack{\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A\\ \operatorname{lcm}(S)=d}}(-1)^{|S|+1},
\qquad d\in\mathcal L(A).
\]
Then
\[
M_A(x)=\sum_{d\in\mathcal L(A)} \lambda_d \Big\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\Big\rfloor,
\qquad
\delta_A=\sum_{d\in\mathcal L(A)}\frac{\lambda_d}{d}.
\]

Define
\[
W_+(A):=\sum_{\lambda_d>0}\lambda_d,\qquad
W_-(A):=\sum_{\lambda_d<0}(-\lambda_d).
\]

#### Lemma B16 (Exact transport identity)
For \(m>n\ge\max(A)\),
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}-2\frac{M_A(n)}{n}
=
-\delta_A
+\sum_{d\in\mathcal L(A)}\lambda_d\!\left(\frac{2}{n}\Big\{\frac{n}{d}\Big\}
-\frac{1}{m}\Big\{\frac{m}{d}\Big\}\right).
\]

**Proof.**
Use \(\lfloor x/d\rfloor=x/d-\{x/d\}\) in \(M_A(x)=\sum_d \lambda_d\lfloor x/d\rfloor\), divide by \(x\), and subtract \(2M_A(n)/n\) from \(M_A(m)/m\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B17 (Signed GL1 upper bound)
For \(m>n\ge\max(A)\),
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}-2\frac{M_A(n)}{n}
\le
-\delta_A+\frac{2W_+(A)}{n}+\frac{W_-(A)}{m}
\le
-\delta_A+\frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
From Lemma B16, bound each term with \(0\le\{x/d\}<1\):

- if \(\lambda_d>0\), then
  \[
  \lambda_d\!\left(\frac{2}{n}\{n/d\}-\frac1m\{m/d\}\right)\le \frac{2\lambda_d}{n};
  \]
- if \(\lambda_d<0\), write \(\lambda_d=-\mu_d\), \(\mu_d>0\), then
  \[
  -\mu_d\!\left(\frac{2}{n}\{n/d\}-\frac1m\{m/d\}\right)\le \frac{\mu_d}{m}.
  \]

Sum over \(d\in\mathcal L(A)\). \(\square\)

#### Corollary B18 (GL1 finite-\(n\) criterion)
If
\[
n>\frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{\delta_A},
\]
then for all \(m>n\),
\[
\frac{|B\cap[1,m]|}{m}<2\,\frac{|B\cap[1,n]|}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
By Lemma B17, RHS is \(<0\) under the stated inequality, hence the target inequality follows. \(\square\)

**Interpretation.**
This is a genuine signed transport inequality: positive and negative lcm-weights contribute asymmetrically (\(2/n\) vs \(1/m\)). It sharpens the crude \(3C_A/\delta_A\) criterion whenever cancellation in lcm-layers makes \(2W_++W_-\ll 3(2^{|A|}-1)\).

### G. GL2 Progress: Near-Extremizer Rigidity (partial, rigorous)

Let
\[
R_A(n,m):=\frac{M_A(m)/m}{M_A(n)/n},\qquad m>n\ge \max(A).
\]

#### Lemma B19 (Near-factor-2 forces a finite window)
Fix finite \(A\), and \(0<\varepsilon<\delta_A\).  
If
\[
R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon,
\]
then necessarily
\[
n<\frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{\delta_A-\varepsilon}.
\]

**Proof.**
From \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\),
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}-2\frac{M_A(n)}{n}
>
-\varepsilon\frac{M_A(n)}{n}
\ge -\varepsilon
\]
since \(M_A(n)/n\le1\).  
By Lemma B17,
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}-2\frac{M_A(n)}{n}
\le
-\delta_A+\frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{n}.
\]
Combining,
\[
-\varepsilon<-\delta_A+\frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{n},
\]
so
\[
n<\frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{\delta_A-\varepsilon}.
\]
\(\square\)

#### Corollary B20 (Uniform exclusion of near-extremizers at large \(n\))
For fixed \(A\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,\delta_A)\), all pairs \(m>n\) with
\[
n\ge \frac{2W_+(A)+W_-(A)}{\delta_A-\varepsilon}
\]
satisfy
\[
R_A(n,m)\le 2-\varepsilon.
\]

**Proof.**
Contrapositive of Lemma B19. \(\square\)

**What this gives for GL2.**
- We now have a rigorous near-extremizer rigidity in the \(n\)-direction: ratio \(>2-\varepsilon\) can occur only in an explicit finite initial window.
- The remaining GL2 gap is structural inside that finite window: prove that any such near-extremizer must be singleton-dominant (or classify all exceptional reduced patterns).

### H. Global Reduction (non-finite, theorem-level)

Let \(G:=A_{\min}\) (Lemma B11), and define
\[
\mu_G:=\sum_{g\in G}\frac1g.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}
\le \sum_{g\in G}\frac{\lfloor m/g\rfloor}{m}
< \sum_{g\in G}\frac1g
=\mu_G,
\]
we get the following exact reduction.

#### Lemma B22 (Single-time reduction)
If
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}\ge \frac{\mu_G}{2},
\]
then for every \(m>n\),
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}<2\,\frac{M_A(n)}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
From \(M_A(m)/m<\mu_G\le 2M_A(n)/n\). \(\square\)

So EP-488 is reduced to proving
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}\ge \frac12\sum_{g\in A_{\min}}\frac1g
\quad(n\ge \max A). \tag{R}
\]

#### Lemma B23 (Bonferroni sufficient condition for (R))
Let
\[
\Omega_G(n):=\sum_{\substack{g,h\in G\\ g<h}}\frac{\lfloor n/\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)\rfloor}{n}.
\]
If
\[
\Omega_G(n)\le \frac{\mu_G}{2}-\frac{|G|}{n},
\]
then (R) holds.

**Proof.**
By two-term inclusion-exclusion,
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}
\ge
\sum_{g\in G}\frac{\lfloor n/g\rfloor}{n}
-\Omega_G(n).
\]
Also \(\lfloor n/g\rfloor/n\ge 1/g-1/n\), so
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}\ge \mu_G-\frac{|G|}{n}-\Omega_G(n)\ge \frac{\mu_G}{2}.
\]
Thus (R) follows. \(\square\)

**Interpretation (new global bottleneck).**
The hard part is now explicit and non-finite:
prove a uniform overlap bound of the shape
\[
\Omega_G(n)\le \frac{\mu_G}{2}-\frac{|G|}{n},
\]
for reduced divisor antichains \(G\). This is a sieve/overlap-control statement, not a finite pattern check.
This condition is a **sufficient criterion**, not currently proved as a universal identity.

#### Lemma B24 (Near-extremizer overlap coercion)
Keep notation
\[
S_1(n):=\sum_{g\in G}\frac{\lfloor n/g\rfloor}{n},\qquad
\Omega_G(n):=\sum_{g<h}\frac{\lfloor n/\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)\rfloor}{n}.
\]
If for some \(m>n\ge \max(A)\),
\[
R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\qquad(0<\varepsilon<1),
\]
then
\[
\Omega_G(n)>S_1(n)-\frac{\mu_G}{2-\varepsilon}.
\]
In particular, since \(S_1(n)\ge \mu_G-|G|/n\),
\[
\Omega_G(n)>
\mu_G\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon}
-\frac{|G|}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
From \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\),
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}>(2-\varepsilon)\frac{M_A(n)}{n}.
\]
But \(M_A(m)/m<\mu_G\), hence
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}<\frac{\mu_G}{2-\varepsilon}. \tag{1}
\]
Also by two-term inclusion-exclusion,
\[
\frac{M_A(n)}{n}\ge S_1(n)-\Omega_G(n). \tag{2}
\]
Combining (1) and (2),
\[
S_1(n)-\Omega_G(n)<\frac{\mu_G}{2-\varepsilon},
\]
which is the first claim. Using \(S_1(n)\ge \mu_G-|G|/n\) gives the second inequality. \(\square\)

**GL2 consequence.**
Any near-factor-2 configuration must exhibit pair-overlap mass at (roughly) half of \(\mu_G\). This turns GL2 into a structural theorem about high-overlap reduced divisor families.

#### Lemma B25 (Anchor overlap mass)
Let
\[
\widetilde\Omega_G:=\sum_{g<h}\frac{1}{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}.
\]
Then there exists \(g_*\in G\) such that
\[
\sum_{h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}}\frac{1}{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}
\ge
\frac{2\widetilde\Omega_G}{|G|}.
\]

**Proof.**
Define
\[
T(g):=\sum_{h\in G\setminus\{g\}}\frac{1}{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{g\in G}T(g)=2\widetilde\Omega_G.
\]
By averaging, some \(g_*\) satisfies \(T(g_*)\ge 2\widetilde\Omega_G/|G|\). \(\square\)

#### Corollary B26 (Near-extremizer anchor from B24)
Assume \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\) \((0<\varepsilon<1)\).  
Set \(r:=|G|\), \(G=A_{\min}\). Then there exists \(g_*\in G\) with
\[
\sum_{h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}}\frac{1}{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}
>
\frac{2}{r}\left(\mu_G\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon}-\frac{|G|}{n}\right).
\]

**Proof.**
By B24,
\[
\Omega_G(n)>
\mu_G\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon}
-\frac{|G|}{n}.
\]
Since \(\lfloor x\rfloor\le x\), we have
\[
\Omega_G(n)\le \widetilde\Omega_G.
\]
Apply Lemma B25. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B27 (Threshold core around anchor)
Let \(g_*\in G\), \(r:=|G|\), and
\[
T_*:=\sum_{h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}}\frac{1}{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}.
\]
For any \(Y>0\), define
\[
N_Y:=\#\{h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}:\ \mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)\le Y\}.
\]
Then
\[
N_Y\ge \frac{Y\,T_*-(r-1)}{Y-1}.
\]

**Proof.**
Split the sum \(T_*\) into terms with lcm \(\le Y\) and \(>Y\):
\[
T_*
\le N_Y\cdot 1 + (r-1-N_Y)\frac1Y
=\frac{r-1}{Y}+N_Y\!\left(1-\frac1Y\right).
\]
Rearranging yields
\[
N_Y\ge \frac{Y T_*-(r-1)}{Y-1},
\]
for \(Y>1\). (For \(0<Y\le1\), the claim is trivial.) \(\square\)

**Structural takeaway (GL2 bridge).**
Near-extremizers force an anchor \(g_*\) with many low-lcm pairs \((g_*,h)\).  
The remaining step to full GL2 is to show that, in a reduced divisor antichain, such a large low-lcm anchor core can only occur in singleton-dominant (or otherwise explicitly classifiable) configurations.

#### Lemma B28 (Anchor factorization identity)
Fix \(g_*\in G\). For each \(h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}\), define
\[
d_h:=\gcd(g_*,h),\qquad
u_h:=\frac{h}{d_h}=\frac{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}{g_*}.
\]
Then \(u_h\in\mathbb N\), \(u_h\ge2\), and
\[
T_*:=\sum_{h\ne g_*}\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}
=\frac1{g_*}\sum_{h\ne g_*}\frac1{u_h}.
\]

**Proof.**
By definition, \(\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)=g_*u_h\), giving the identity.
If \(u_h=1\), then \(h=d_h\mid g_*\), impossible in reduced \(G\). So \(u_h\ge2\). \(\square\)

#### Corollary B29 (Universal anchor upper bound)
With notation of B28,
\[
T_*\le \frac{r-1}{2g_*}.
\]

**Proof.**
From B28, \(u_h\ge2\), hence each term \(1/u_h\le1/2\). \(\square\)

#### Corollary B30 (Near-extremizer quantitative constraint)
If \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\) \((0<\varepsilon<1)\), then for the anchor \(g_*\) from B26,
\[
\mu_G\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon}
<
\frac{r(r-1)}{4g_*}+\frac{r}{n}.
\]

**Proof.**
From B26,
\[
T_*>
\frac{2}{r}\left(\mu_G\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon}-\frac{r}{n}\right).
\]
From B29, \(T_*\le (r-1)/(2g_*)\). Combine and rearrange. \(\square\)

**Interpretation.**
Near-extremizers require an anchor \(g_*\) small enough (relative to \(\mu_G,r,n\)) to satisfy B30.  
This is a genuine structural restriction and narrows GL2 to controlling reduced families with such a forced anchor scale.

#### Lemma B31 (Anchor gcd-decomposition)
Fix \(g\in G\), and write
\[
\mu_{-g}:=\sum_{h\in G\setminus\{g\}}\frac1h,\qquad
H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g):=\sum_{\substack{h\in G\setminus\{g\}\\ \gcd(g,h)>1}}\frac1h.
\]
Then
\[
T(g):=\sum_{h\ne g}\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}
\le
\frac{\mu_{-g}}{g}+\Bigl(1-\frac1g\Bigr)H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g).
\]

**Proof.**
Using \(\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)=gh/\gcd(g,h)\),
\[
\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}=\frac{\gcd(g,h)}{gh}.
\]
If \(\gcd(g,h)=1\), this equals \(1/(gh)\).  
If \(\gcd(g,h)>1\), then \(\gcd(g,h)\le g\), so
\[
\frac{\gcd(g,h)}{gh}\le \frac1h.
\]
Summing over coprime and non-coprime parts gives
\[
T(g)\le \frac{\mu_{-g}-H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g)}{g}+H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g),
\]
which is the claim. \(\square\)

#### Corollary B32 (Near-extremizer forces non-coprime anchor mass)
Assume \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\) and let \(g_*\) be the anchor from B26.  
Define
\[
L_*:=\frac{2}{r}\left(\mu_G\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon}-\frac{r}{n}\right),
\quad
\mu_*:=\mu_G-\frac1{g_*}.
\]
Then
\[
H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g_*)
\ge
\frac{L_*-\mu_*/g_*}{1-1/g_*}.
\]

**Proof.**
B26 gives \(T(g_*)>L_*\).  
Apply Lemma B31 with \(g=g_*\): if \(T(g_*)>L_*\), then
\[
L_*<
\frac{\mu_*}{g_*}+\Bigl(1-\frac1{g_*}\Bigr)H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g_*),
\]
and rearrange. \(\square\)

**GL2 refinement.**
Near-extremizers do not only require a small anchor; they require a quantitatively large harmonic mass of generators sharing factors with that anchor.  
This pushes the remaining GL2 step toward a prime-factor incidence theorem on reduced divisor antichains.

#### Lemma B33 (Prime-fiber reduction from anchor mass)
Let \(g_*\in G\), and let \(P(g_*)\) be the set of primes dividing \(g_*\).
For each \(p\in P(g_*)\), define
\[
H_p(g_*):=\sum_{\substack{h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}\\ p\mid h}}\frac1h.
\]
Then
\[
H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g_*)\le \sum_{p\mid g_*} H_p(g_*).
\]
Consequently, there exists \(p_*\mid g_*\) such that
\[
H_{p_*}(g_*)\ge \frac{H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g_*)}{\omega(g_*)},
\]
where \(\omega(g_*)\) is the number of distinct prime factors of \(g_*\).

**Proof.**
If \(\gcd(g_*,h)>1\), then \(h\) is divisible by at least one prime \(p\mid g_*\). Thus
\[
1_{\gcd(g_*,h)>1}\le \sum_{p\mid g_*}1_{p\mid h}.
\]
Multiply by \(1/h\), sum over \(h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}\), getting the first inequality.  
The second is the pigeonhole principle over at most \(\omega(g_*)\) prime fibers. \(\square\)

#### Corollary B34 (Near-extremizer heavy prime fiber)
Under the near-extremizer hypothesis \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\), there exists \(p_*\mid g_*\) such that
\[
H_{p_*}(g_*)
\ge
\frac{1}{\omega(g_*)}
\cdot
\frac{L_*-\mu_*/g_*}{1-1/g_*},
\]
with \(L_*,\mu_*\) as in B32.

**Proof.**
Combine B32 and B33. \(\square\)

**Current GL2 bottleneck (fully explicit).**
To finish GL2, it now suffices to prove a nontrivial upper bound on \(H_p(g)\) for reduced divisor antichains \(G\), strong enough to contradict B34 in the near-extremizer regime.

#### Lemma B35 (Prime anchor exclusion in near-extremizers)
Assume \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\) and let \(g_*\) be the anchor from B26.
If \(g_*\) is prime, then necessarily
\[
L_*\le \frac{\mu_*}{g_*},
\]
where \(L_*,\mu_*\) are as in B32.
Hence, whenever \(L_*>\mu_*/g_*\), the anchor \(g_*\) cannot be prime.

**Proof.**
If \(g_*=p\) prime and \(h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}\) satisfies \(\gcd(g_*,h)>1\), then \(p\mid h\), so \(g_*=p\mid h\), impossible because \(G\) is reduced (no divisibility among distinct generators). Therefore
\[
H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g_*)=0.
\]
Applying B32:
\[
0=H_{\mathrm{nc}}(g_*)\ge \frac{L_*-\mu_*/g_*}{1-1/g_*},
\]
which implies \(L_*\le\mu_*/g_*\). \(\square\)

**Structural consequence.**
Near-extremizer analysis can be restricted to composite anchors \(g_*\) (and, more specifically, to anchors with enough prime-factor incidence to support the B32 lower bound).

#### Lemma B36 (Prime-power anchor exclusion criterion)
Assume \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\), and let \(g_*=p^k\) (\(p\) prime, \(k\ge2\)) be the anchor.
Then
\[
L_*\le \frac{\mu_*}{p}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{no contradiction from B32,}
\]
while
\[
L_*>\frac{\mu_*}{p}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
g_*=p^k\ \text{is impossible}.
\]

**Proof.**
For any \(h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}\),
\[
\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}
=\frac{\gcd(g_*,h)}{g_*h}
\le \frac{1}{h}.
\]
Because \(G\) is reduced, \(h\) cannot be a multiple of \(g_*=p^k\), so \(\gcd(g_*,h)\) is a proper divisor of \(p^k\), hence
\[
\gcd(g_*,h)\le p^{k-1}=g_*/p.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g_*,h)}\le \frac1{ph},
\]
and summing over \(h\in G\setminus\{g_*\}\):
\[
T(g_*)\le \frac{\mu_*}{p}.
\]
By B26/B32, near-extremizer lower bound gives \(T(g_*)>L_*\). So \(L_*>\mu_*/p\) is impossible. \(\square\)

**Note.**
This criterion reduces the remaining GL2 branch to composite anchors where \(L_*\le \mu_*/p\) for every prime \(p\mid g_*\), i.e. anchors with sufficiently rich multi-prime incidence.

#### Lemma B37 (Unified anchor contraction bound)
Let \(g\in G\), and let
\[
p_{\min}(g):=\min\{p\ \text{prime}: p\mid g\},\qquad
\mu_{-g}:=\sum_{h\in G\setminus\{g\}}\frac1h.
\]
Then
\[
T(g):=\sum_{h\ne g}\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}
\le
\frac{\mu_{-g}}{p_{\min}(g)}.
\]

**Proof.**
For \(h\in G\setminus\{g\}\), reducedness implies \(g\nmid h\), hence
\[
\gcd(g,h)<g.
\]
Any proper divisor of \(g\) is at most \(g/p_{\min}(g)\), so
\[
\gcd(g,h)\le \frac{g}{p_{\min}(g)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac1{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}
=\frac{\gcd(g,h)}{gh}
\le \frac{1}{p_{\min}(g)\,h}.
\]
Summing over \(h\ne g\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

#### Corollary B38 (Unified near-extremizer anchor exclusion)
Under \(R_A(n,m)>2-\varepsilon\), for the anchor \(g_*\) from B26,
\[
L_*\le \frac{\mu_*}{p_{\min}(g_*)}.
\]
Hence any parameter regime forcing
\[
L_*>\frac{\mu_*}{p_{\min}(g_*)}
\]
is impossible.

**Proof.**
B26 gives \(T(g_*)>L_*\), while B37 gives \(T(g_*)\le \mu_*/p_{\min}(g_*)\). \(\square\)

**Update of GL2 bottleneck.**
The remaining branch is exactly where
\[
L_*\le \frac{\mu_*}{p_{\min}(g_*)}
\]
and simultaneously B34 forces a large prime-fiber mass.  
Finishing GL2 amounts to proving these two constraints are incompatible except in singleton-dominant structure.

### I. Counterexample Profile (exact-\(2\) regime)

Assume, for contradiction, there is a violating pair \(m>n\ge\max(A)\) with
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}\ge 2\frac{M_A(n)}{n}. \tag{CE}
\]
Then all prior near-extremizer lemmas apply with \(\varepsilon=0\).

Set \(r:=|G|\), \(G=A_{\min}\), and choose anchor \(g_*\) from B26.
Then
\[
L_*=\frac{2}{r}\left(\frac{\mu_G}{2}-\frac{r}{n}\right)=\frac{\mu_G}{r}-\frac{2}{n}.
\]

#### Lemma B39 (Necessary anchor inequalities for a true counterexample)
Under (CE), the anchor \(g_*\) must satisfy
\[
\frac{\mu_G}{r}-\frac{2}{n}
\le
\frac{\mu_G-\frac1{g_*}}{p_{\min}(g_*)}, \tag{N1}
\]
\[
\mu_G\frac12
\le
\frac{r(r-1)}{4g_*}+\frac{r}{n}, \tag{N2}
\]
and there exists \(p_*\mid g_*\) with
\[
H_{p_*}(g_*)
\ge
\frac{1}{\omega(g_*)}
\cdot
\frac{\left(\frac{\mu_G}{r}-\frac{2}{n}\right)-\frac{\mu_G-\frac1{g_*}}{g_*}}
{1-1/g_*}. \tag{N3}
\]

**Proof.**
(N1) is B38 at \(\varepsilon=0\).  
(N2) is B30 at \(\varepsilon=0\).  
(N3) is B34 at \(\varepsilon=0\). \(\square\)

#### Corollary B40 (Asymptotic shape of any counterexample sequence)
For any sequence of hypothetical counterexamples with \(n\to\infty\), one must have eventually
\[
\frac{\mu_G}{r}\lesssim \frac{\mu_G}{p_{\min}(g_*)},
\]
hence
\[
p_{\min}(g_*)\lesssim r.
\]

**Proof.**
From (N1), as \(n\to\infty\), correction \(2/n\to0\), and \((\mu_G-1/g_*)/p_{\min}\le \mu_G/p_{\min}\). \(\square\)

**Meaning.**
Any true counterexample is forced into a narrow arithmetic corridor:
- anchor must be small enough to satisfy (N2),
- smallest anchor prime factor cannot be too large relative to \(r\) (B40),
- and one prime-fiber harmonic mass must be large (N3).
The remaining proof task is to show this corridor is empty for reduced antichains.

#### Lemma B42 (Quantitative exclusion when \(p_{\min}(g_*)>r\))
Assume the exact-counterexample regime (CE), and let \(g_*\) be the anchor from B39 with
\[
p:=p_{\min}(g_*),\qquad p>r.
\]
Then
\[
n<\frac{2}{\mu_G\left(\frac1r-\frac1p\right)}.
\]
In particular, if \(p\ge r+1\), then
\[
n<\frac{2r(r+1)}{\mu_G}.
\]

**Proof.**
From (N1),
\[
\frac{\mu_G}{r}-\frac{2}{n}\le \frac{\mu_G-\frac1{g_*}}{p}\le \frac{\mu_G}{p}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mu_G\left(\frac1r-\frac1p\right)\le \frac{2}{n},
\]
which gives the first claim.  
For \(p\ge r+1\),
\[
\frac1r-\frac1p\ge \frac1r-\frac1{r+1}=\frac1{r(r+1)},
\]
yielding the second bound. \(\square\)

**Consequence.**
Any infinite family of counterexamples must lie in the branch
\[
p_{\min}(g_*)\le r
\]
eventually; the \(p_{\min}(g_*)>r\) branch is quantitatively finite.

#### Lemma B43 (Prime-fiber packing upper bound)
Let \(G\) be reduced, \(g\in G\), and let \(p\mid g\) be prime. Then
\[
H_p(g):=\sum_{\substack{h\in G\setminus\{g\}\\ p\mid h}}\frac1h
\le \frac{r-1}{2p},
\qquad r:=|G|.
\]

**Proof.**
If \(h\in G\setminus\{g\}\) and \(p\mid h\), then \(h\neq p\): otherwise \(h=p\mid g\), contradicting reducedness (distinct generators cannot divide each other). Hence \(h\ge 2p\), so each term \(1/h\le 1/(2p)\). There are at most \(r-1\) such terms. \(\square\)

#### Corollary B44 (Residual-branch necessary inequality)
In the exact-counterexample regime (CE), for the prime \(p_*\mid g_*\) from B34,
\[
\frac{1}{\omega(g_*)}
\cdot
\frac{\left(\frac{\mu_G}{r}-\frac{2}{n}\right)-\frac{\mu_G-\frac1{g_*}}{g_*}}
{1-1/g_*}
\le
\frac{r-1}{2p_*}.
\]

**Proof.**
Lower bound from B34, upper bound from B43. \(\square\)

**Residual branch now.**
Together with B42, any hypothetical infinite counterexample family must satisfy simultaneously:
\[
p_{\min}(g_*)\le r,\quad \text{and}\quad \text{B44}.
\]
So the last step is a structural contradiction theorem for reduced antichains in this low-prime, bounded-incidence corridor.

### J. Density Split (global simplification)

Write
\[
D(x):=\frac{M_A(x)}{x}.
\]

#### Lemma B41 (Dense-\(n\) case is automatic)
If \(D(n)\ge \frac12\), then for every \(m>n\),
\[
D(m)<2D(n).
\]

**Proof.**
Since \(1\notin A\), not every integer is divisible by an element of \(A\), hence \(D(m)<1\) for all \(m\).
If \(D(n)\ge1/2\), then \(2D(n)\ge1\), so \(D(m)<1\le2D(n)\). \(\square\)

So EP-488 reduces to the sparse regime
\[
D(n)<\frac12. \tag{S}
\]

#### Reduction target in sparse regime
Let \(G=A_{\min}\), \(r:=|G|\), and
\[
I(n):=\sum_{g\in G}\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{g}\Big\rfloor,\qquad M:=M_A(n).
\]
Because
\[
\sum_{g\in G}\frac1g
\le \sum_{g\in G}\frac{\lfloor n/g\rfloor+1}{n}
=\frac{I(n)+r}{n},
\]
a sufficient condition for EP-488 (via Lemma B22) is
\[
I(n)+r\le 2M. \tag{K}
\]
Indeed then \(\mu_G\le 2M/n\), and for all \(m>n\),
\[
\frac{M_A(m)}{m}<\mu_G\le 2\frac{M_A(n)}{n}.
\]

**Final bottleneck reformulated.**
After B41, it suffices to prove (K) for all reduced \(G\) in the sparse regime (S).  
This is a purely combinatorial incidence inequality and would complete the full theorem.

#### Lemma B45 (Equivalent forms of the sparse bottleneck)
Let
\[
\deg_G(x):=\#\{g\in G:\ g\mid x\},
\]
and define
\[
\mathrm{Dup}:=\sum_{1\le x\le n,\ \deg_G(x)\ge1}\bigl(\deg_G(x)-1\bigr),
\qquad
N_{\mathrm{nb}}:=M_A(n)-r.
\]
Then the condition (K)
\[
I(n)+r\le 2M_A(n)
\]
is equivalent to each of:
\[
\mathrm{Dup}\le N_{\mathrm{nb}}, \tag{K1}
\]
\[
\sum_{x\le n,\ \deg_G(x)\ge1}\deg_G(x)\le 2M_A(n)-r. \tag{K2}
\]

**Proof.**
By definition
\[
I(n)=\sum_{x\le n}\deg_G(x),
\qquad
\mathrm{Dup}=I(n)-M_A(n).
\]
Hence
\[
I(n)+r\le 2M_A(n)
\iff I(n)-M_A(n)\le M_A(n)-r
\iff \mathrm{Dup}\le N_{\mathrm{nb}}.
\]
This also gives (K2). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B46 (Pair-overlap sufficient criterion for (K))
Define pair-overlap incidence
\[
P(n):=\sum_{g<h}\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{\mathrm{lcm}(g,h)}\Big\rfloor
=\sum_{x\le n}\binom{\deg_G(x)}{2}.
\]
If
\[
P(n)\le N_{\mathrm{nb}},
\]
then (K) holds.

**Proof.**
For each \(d\ge1\), \(\binom d2\ge d-1\). Summing over \(x\le n\):
\[
P(n)=\sum_x \binom{\deg_G(x)}2
\ge \sum_x (\deg_G(x)-1)_+
=\mathrm{Dup}.
\]
Thus \(P(n)\le N_{\mathrm{nb}}\) implies \(\mathrm{Dup}\le N_{\mathrm{nb}}\), i.e. (K1), hence (K). \(\square\)

**Important correction.**
The condition \(P(n)\le M_A(n)-r\) is only sufficient, not necessary, and it is false in general even under sparse density \(D(n)<1/2\).  
Counterexample:
\[
G=\{4,6,9,10,14,15\},\quad n=60,
\]
for which
\[
D(n)=\frac{27}{60}<\frac12,\qquad
P(n)=23,\qquad
M_A(n)-r=27-6=21.
\]
So \(P(n)>M_A(n)-r\), yet EP-488 still holds for this instance.

Therefore the true remaining theorem target is (K) itself:
\[
I(n)+r\le 2M_A(n)
\]
in sparse regime, without replacing it by the stronger \(P\)-bound.

#### Lemma B47 (Order-slack identity for (K))
Fix any ordering \(G=\{g_1,\dots,g_r\}\). Let
\[
u_i:=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{g_i}\Big\rfloor,\qquad
t_i:=\#\Bigl(g_i\mathbb N\cap[1,n]\setminus \bigcup_{j<i} g_j\mathbb N\Bigr).
\]
Then
\[
I(n)=\sum_{i=1}^r u_i,\qquad
M_A(n)=\sum_{i=1}^r t_i,
\]
and
\[
2M_A(n)-I(n)-r
=
\sum_{i=1}^r\bigl(2t_i-u_i-1\bigr). \tag{S}
\]
Hence (K) is equivalent to nonnegativity of the total slack in (S).

**Proof.**
Immediate from definitions of \(I,M\). \(\square\)

#### Corollary B48 (Local-to-global sufficient criterion)
If there exists an ordering with
\[
t_i\ge \frac{u_i+1}{2}\quad\text{for all }i,
\]
then (K) holds.

**Proof.**
Each summand \(2t_i-u_i-1\ge0\), so (S) is nonnegative. \(\square\)

**Deep remaining target (current best).**
Prove existence of such an ordering (or a weaker averaged variant implying (S)\(\ge0\)) for reduced antichains in sparse regime \(D(n)<1/2\).  
This would finish EP-488 from B41.

#### Open Lemma OL1 (Order-slack existence, exact form)
For every reduced \(G\) and \(n\ge \max G\) with \(D(n)<1/2\), there exists an ordering \(g_1,\dots,g_r\) such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^r(2t_i-u_i-1)\ge0
\]
(equivalently \(I(n)+r\le 2M_A(n)\)).

This is exactly equivalent to the remaining sparse-case theorem.

#### Why current inequalities still fall short
Current global constraints (B39–B44) force a narrow counterexample corridor but do not yet imply OL1:
- B38 gives anchor contraction \(L_*\le \mu_*/p_{\min}(g_*)\),
- B44 gives a prime-fiber incidence inequality,
- B42 makes \(p_{\min}>r\) quantitatively finite.

These are necessary constraints, but not yet contradictory in the residual branch \(p_{\min}(g_*)\le r\).

#### Next-proof directions from OL1
1. Prove OL1 via a deterministic ordering rule (descending/greedy maximum new mass) with an averaged slack estimate.
2. Prove a direct inequality \(\mathrm{Dup}\le N_{\mathrm{nb}}\) from divisor-incidence decomposition by prime fibers.
3. Strengthen B44 with a sharper \(H_p\)-upper bound that uses reducedness + sparse density simultaneously (not only \(h\ge 2p\)).

If A supplies finite witnesses above \(k\) in growing regions, compactness (or direct embedding) yields global lower bound \(>k\).

\[
\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta)=\Re S_A(\theta).

\[
\int_0^{2\pi}\Re S_A(\theta)\,d\theta=0.
\]

**Proof.**
Integral of each \(\cos(n\theta)\) over a full period is zero. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies negative dip)
If A controls \(\|S_A\|_2\) and higher moments to preclude concentration on positive side, then there exists \(\theta\) with \(\Re S_A(\theta)\le -c\sqrt N\).

**Proof.**
Mean-zero plus moment bounds force nontrivial negative tail by Paley–Zygmund/Chebyshev-type arguments on centered variable. \(\square\)

### C. Main unresolved point

The bottleneck is deriving moment bounds uniform over all sets \(A\), including highly structured additive sets where cancellation is weakest.

with \(\chi(G)\ge f(k)\) contains an odd cycle whose vertex set spans a subgraph of
chromatic number at least \(k\)?
literature:
## Literature
- This is an odd-cycle/chromatic amplification question: high global chromatic number versus high chromatic complexity already visible on vertices of one odd cycle.
- No definitive function \(f\) is recorded in the local dataset entry.
computation:
## Our Approaches / What Is Proven
- Used Mycielski graphs \(M^t(C_5)\), which are triangle-free with known chromatic numbers \(3+t\), as structured stress tests.

- For \(t=0\) to \(5\), global chromatic level rises from 3 to 8 as expected.

## Added Proof Layer (No New Computation)
### One-Dimensional Case (Closed)
Let \(A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_n\}\subset\mathbb R\) with all pairwise distances at least
1 apart from each other (equivalently, all differences \(a_j-a_i\), \(i<j\), are
distinct). Then there are \(\binom n2\) distinct positive differences, each at
least \(1\), so the largest difference is at least \(\binom n2\):
\[
\operatorname{diam}(A)=a_n-a_1\ge \binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{diam}(A)\gg n^2\), which gives the required quadratic scale
in \(d=1\) (as recorded in the literature).

### Remaining Open Part
For fixed \(d\ge2\), need asymptotically sharp lower bounds approaching
\((1+o(1))n^2\).

### Blocking Lemma
- Need a high-dimensional incidence/energy theorem that converts distance
  separation constraints into near-maximal diameter growth, matching the
  one-dimensional quadratic scale up to \(1+o(1)\).

## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
For fixed \(d\ge2\), prove
\[
\operatorname{diam}(A)\ge (1+o(1))n^2
\]
under pairwise-distance separation.

### Step A: Additive-Energy Suppression
Show distance-separation imposes strong anti-concentration on difference vectors,
forcing large spread in projected distances.

### Step B: Projection Rigidity
Find projection direction where 1D shadow retains near-distinct differences for
a large fraction of pairs.

### Step C: Lift Back to Diameter
Use 1D lower bound from Step B to force full \(d\)-dimensional diameter at
\((1+o(1))n^2\) scale.

### Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)
Need a projection lemma: for any such \(A\subset\mathbb R^d\), there exists a
direction \(u\) with at most \(o(n^2)\) collisions among projected pairwise
differences \(\langle a_i-a_j,u\rangle\).

## Added Proof Layer (No New Computation)
### Closed Substatement
The divergence claim
\[
\max_m\bigl(f(n,m)-f(n,n)\bigr)\to\infty
\]
is now proved in the cited 2026 update, so that part is closed.

### Remaining Open Substatement
The near-linear upper-growth target
\[
\max_m f(n,m)\le n^{1+o(1)}
\]
remains open.

### Blocking Lemma
- Need a uniform interval matching theorem controlling the worst-case local
  divisibility assignment overhead in terms of \(n^{o(1)}\), not just existence
  of feasible matchings.

## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
Prove
\[
\max_m f(n,m)\le n^{1+o(1)}.
\]

### Step A: Hall-Defect Bound at Scale \(L\)
For intervals of length \(L\), bound Hall deficits for the bipartite graph
(positions vs divisibility classes) by \(L^{1-\eta}\) uniformly in \(m\).

### Step B: Defect Repair with Sparse Augmentation
Show every deficit can be repaired by enlarging interval length by only
\(L^{o(1)}\), giving feasible perfect matching for the divisibility assignment.

### Step C: Optimize \(L\sim n\)
Set \(L\) near \(n\) and iterate multi-scale repairs to derive
\[
f(n,m)\le n\cdot n^{o(1)}
\]
uniformly in \(m\).

### Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)
Need a near-optimal Hall-uniformity statement for residue-class availability in
arbitrary shifted intervals:
\[
\forall S\subseteq [n],\quad |N_m(S)|\ge |S|-o(n),
\]
uniformly in \(m\), with an error term summable across scales.

### Method Directions
- Dense matching + additive combinatorics in shifted interval residue systems.
- Tao-style transference from average divisor availability to worst-case subsets.
- Randomized nibble/LLL repair of residual unmatched classes.

problem: Are there infinitely many `n!=m` such that `C(2n,n)` and `C(2m,m)` have the same prime-divisor set?
computation:
## Computation in this attempt
I ran exact support-tracking from the recurrence (not heuristic hashing) at large scale.

Data file:
- `data/ep730_large_consecutive_scan.json`
- `data/ep726_ep730_ep731_scan.json` (`ep730` section, small-range cross-check)

Findings:
- Up to `n=2,500,000`, found `25,547` consecutive pairs `(n,n+1)` with equal support.
- Density in buckets stabilizes near `~1%` (for example `20,320` hits up to `2,000,000`).
- First hits recover known small examples (`87,88`, `607,608`) and continue densely afterward.

## Interpretation
This is very strong finite evidence for infinitude, but still not a proof.
Hard point: turning the local recurrence support conditions into a deterministic infinite-family
construction (or a theorem guaranteeing infinitely many `n` with no support toggles).
attempt:
## Rigorous reduction used in this attempt
Let `B_n = C(2n,n)`. Then

`B_{n+1} = B_n * 2(2n+1)/(n+1)`.

So support change from `n` to `n+1` is controlled exactly by prime factors of `2n+1` and `n+1`.
For the special family `n=2^m-1`, this becomes

`B_{2^m} = B_{2^m-1} * (2^{m+1}-1)/2^{m-1}`.

Hence odd-prime support equality for `(2^m-1,2^m)` is equivalent to:
every odd prime divisor of `2^{m+1}-1` already divides `B_{2^m-1}`.

attempt:
## Core reduction used
`H(n)=3` is exactly equivalent to

`gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1`,

since `l=3` forces `k=2`.

Define for each prime `p>3`:

`m_p := lcm(ord_p(2), ord_p(3))`.

Then the equivalent arithmetic form is:

`H(n)=3  <=>  n` is not divisible by any `m_p`.

Reason: `p | gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1)` iff both orders divide `n`, i.e. iff `m_p | n`.

## Conditional theorem (proved as reduction)
If the divisor-moduli family `{m_p : p>3}` is not a covering system of the positive integers
(equivalently: infinitely many `n` avoid all `m_p`), then `H(n)=3` infinitely often.

So the infinitude problem is reduced to a covering-system question for `{m_p}`.

# EP-854 partial theorem: fixed even gaps occur for all sufficiently large primorial levels

Let
`P_k = p_1 p_2 ... p_k`
be the `k`-th primorial, and let
`1=a_1<...<a_{phi(P_k)}=P_k-1`
be the reduced residues modulo `P_k` in increasing order.

Define a gap value `t` to be represented if there exists `j` with
`a_{j+1}-a_j=t`.

## Theorem (proved here)
For every fixed even integer `t>=2`, there exists `k_0(t)` such that for all
`k>=k_0(t)`, the gap `t` is represented among consecutive reduced residues
modulo `P_k`.

### Proof
Write `t=2d`.

Choose `d-1` distinct odd primes
`q_1,...,q_{d-1}` with `q_i>t` among `{p_1,...,p_k}`.
(This is possible for all sufficiently large `k`.)

We construct `x (mod P_k)` by congruences:

1. `x ≡ 1 (mod 2)` (so `x` is odd).
2. For each `i=1,...,d-1`:
   `x ≡ -2i (mod q_i)`.
   Then `x+2i` is divisible by `q_i`.
3. For every other odd prime `p<=p_k` not among `q_i`, choose
   `x ≡ r_p (mod p)` with `r_p` avoiding both `0` and `-t (mod p)`.
   This is always possible since at most two residues are forbidden.

Because moduli are distinct primes, CRT gives a unique class modulo `P_k`
for each such residue-choice family.

For any class produced:
- Endpoints `x` and `x+t` are coprime to `P_k`:
  - modulo `2`, both are odd;
  - modulo each `q_i>t`, `x ≡ -2i` so neither `x` nor `x+t` is `0 mod q_i`
    (since `0<2i<t<q_i`);
  - modulo other odd primes, we explicitly avoided `0` and `-t`.
- Every interior point `x+s` (`1<=s<=t-1`) is non-coprime:
  - if `s` is odd, `x+s` is even;
  - if `s=2i` is even, `x+s = x+2i ≡ 0 (mod q_i)`.

So in the cyclic order modulo `P_k`, `x` and `x+t` are consecutive reduced
residues.

To ensure a **non-wrapping linear** gap in `[1,P_k-1]`, count classes:
for each unused odd prime `p`, number of allowed residues is
`p-ν_p`, where `ν_p in {1,2}`.
Hence number of CRT classes with the above property is
`A_k = Π_{p unused}(p-ν_p)`.
With `t` fixed and `k` increasing, `A_k -> infinity` (new odd primes contribute
factors at least `p-2 > 1`).
Only the last `t` residues in `[0,P_k-1]` can produce wrapping (`x+t >= P_k`),
so once `A_k > t`, at least one class yields `1<=x<=P_k-t-1`.
For that `x`, `x` and `x+t` are consecutive in the linear list, giving gap `t`.

Thus for every fixed even `t`, gap `t` appears for all sufficiently large `k`.
`□`

## Corollary
If `m_k` denotes the smallest even integer not represented as a consecutive
reduced-residue gap modulo `P_k`, then `m_k -> infinity`.

So the first EP-854 sub-question has a positive asymptotic direction:
the first missing even gap must drift to infinity with `k`.

## Limits
This does **not** resolve the stronger quantitative part asking whether the
number of represented even gaps is `≫ max_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)`.

## Claim (historical, stronger than current EP-854 statement)
For primorial modulus `n_k`, every even `t <= max_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)` occurs as a
consecutive reduced-residue gap `a_{j+1}-a_j`.

## Counterexample at `k=6`
Take
`n_6 = 2*3*5*7*11*13 = 30030`,
and let
`1=a_1<a_2<...<a_{phi(n_6)}=n_6-1`
be integers coprime to `n_6`.

Exact computation gives:
- `phi(n_6)=5760`;
- maximum consecutive gap is `22`;
- even gap values present up to `22` are
  `{2,4,6,8,10,12,14,16,18,22}`;
- `20` is missing.

Hence not all even values up to the maximum gap occur.
So the historical "all-even-up-to-max" conjecture is false.

## Theorem A (explicit, all k>=4)
For every `k>=4`, every even `t` with `2<=t<=k` is represented.

### Proof
Write `t=2d`.

We use the same endpoint/interior forcing pattern as before:
- odd interior offsets are killed by parity (`x` odd),
- even interior offsets `2,4,...,2d-2` are killed by distinct odd primes.

Choose `d-1` distinct odd primes
`q_1,...,q_{d-1}` from `{p_1,...,p_k}` such that:
- `q_i > t`,
- `q_i != p_k`.

This is possible because we need `d-1=t/2-1` primes, while the number of
primes `>t` among `p_1,...,p_k` except `p_k` is
`k-pi(t)-1`.
So it suffices that `k-pi(t) >= t/2`.
For `t<=k`, we have `k-pi(t) >= t-pi(t) >= t/2` since `pi(t)<=t/2` for `t>=2`.

Impose congruences:
1. `x ≡ 1 (mod 2)`.
2. `x ≡ -2i (mod q_i)` for `i=1,...,d-1`.
3. For each odd prime `p<=p_k`, `p!=q_i`, `p!=p_k`, choose
   `x ≡ r_p (mod p)` with `r_p` avoiding `0` and `-t (mod p)`.
4. Leave `x (mod p_k)` free, except avoid `0` and `-t (mod p_k)`.

CRT gives one residue class mod `P_k` for each allowed choice of `x (mod p_k)`,
so we get exactly `p_k-2` classes.

For any such class:
- `x` and `x+t` are coprime to `P_k` (by avoided residues);
- each odd interior `x+s` is even;
- each even interior `x+2i` (`1<=i<=d-1`) is divisible by `q_i`.
Hence `x` and `x+t` are consecutive reduced residues in cyclic order.

To get a non-wrapping linear gap, note:
- at most `t` classes can have representative `x > P_k-t-1`;
- but `p_k-2 > t` for `k>=4` and `t<=k`, because `p_k > k+2`:
  among `2,3,...,k+2` there are `k+1` integers and at least two composites
  (`4,6`), so at most `k-1` primes there; thus the `k`-th prime exceeds `k+2`.

Therefore at least one class has `1<=x<=P_k-t-1`, yielding
`a_{j+1}-a_j=t`. `□`

## Theorem B (asymptotic strengthening)
For every `epsilon>0`, there exists `k_0(epsilon)` such that for all
`k>=k_0(epsilon)`, every even `t` with `2<=t<=(2-epsilon)k` is represented.

### Proof sketch
Repeat Theorem A, with the same sufficient conditions:
1. enough primes above `t`: `k-pi(t) >= t/2`;
2. enough free classes to avoid wrap: `p_k-2 > t`.

For `t<=(2-epsilon)k`,
`pi(t) <= pi((2-epsilon)k)`.
By `pi(x)=o(x)`, for large `k`,
`pi((2-epsilon)k) <= (epsilon/2)k`,
so
`k-pi(t) >= (1-epsilon/2)k >= t/2`.

Also `p_k/k -> infinity` (equivalently from PNT for `p_k`), so for large `k`,
`p_k > (2-epsilon)k + 2 >= t+2`, hence `p_k-2>t`.

Thus Theorem A's construction works uniformly for all even
`t<=(2-epsilon)k` once `k` is large. `□`

## Consequences
- Number of represented even gap values is at least `floor(k/2)` for every `k>=4`.
- More strongly, for every fixed `epsilon>0` and large `k`, at least
  `floor((2-epsilon)k/2)` even values are represented.
- This is strictly stronger than "fixed `t` eventually represented".

## Limit
This still does not settle the EP-854 quantitative target
`#represented even gaps >> max gap`, because it does not provide a matching
upper bound on `max gap` in terms of `k`.

## What is resolved

initial all-even-up-to-max-gap expectation fails already at n_k=2*3*5*7*11*13.

## Weaker Quantitative Theorem (Lemma by Lemma)
Let
\[
R_k:=\#\{\text{even gap sizes represented among consecutive reduced residues mod }P_k\},
\]
and let
\[
G_k:=\max\{\text{consecutive reduced-residue gap mod }P_k\}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Weaker quantitative bound]
For all sufficiently large \(k\),
\[
R_k \gg \frac{\log G_k}{\log\log G_k}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}
For every \(k\ge 4\),
\[
R_k\ge \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem A above, every even \(t\) with \(2\le t\le k\) is represented.
There are exactly \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) such even integers.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
For every \(k\),
\[
G_k\le P_k-1< P_k.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
All reduced residues are in \([1,P_k-1]\), so every consecutive difference is at
most \(P_k-1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
\[
\log P_k \asymp k\log k.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(P_k=\prod_{i\le k}p_i\),
\[
\log P_k=\sum_{i\le k}\log p_i=\vartheta(p_k),
\]
where \(\vartheta\) is the Chebyshev theta function. By the prime number theorem,
\(\vartheta(x)\sim x\) and \(p_k\sim k\log k\). Hence
\(\log P_k\asymp k\log k\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
For all sufficiently large \(k\),
\[
k \gg \frac{\log P_k}{\log\log P_k}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
From \(\log P_k\asymp k\log k\), we get \(\log\log P_k\asymp \log k\). Therefore
\[
\frac{\log P_k}{\log\log P_k}\asymp \frac{k\log k}{\log k}\asymp k.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
For all sufficiently large \(k\),
\[
k \gg \frac{\log G_k}{\log\log G_k}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \(G_k<P_k\), we have \(\log G_k\le \log P_k\). For large \(x\), the function
\(x/\log x\) is increasing, so
\[
\frac{\log G_k}{\log\log G_k}
\le
\frac{\log P_k}{\log\log P_k}
\ll k
\]
by the previous lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the theorem]
From Lemma 1,
\[
R_k\ge \left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\right\rfloor \gg k.
\]
From Lemma 5,
\[
k \gg \frac{\log G_k}{\log\log G_k}.
\]
Combining,
\[
R_k \gg \frac{\log G_k}{\log\log G_k}.
\]
\end{proof}

This is weaker than the target \(R_k\gg G_k\), but it is a fully rigorous
quantitative consequence of the currently proved ingredients.

## Added Direct Proof (As Written)
Take the nonzero entire function
\[
f(z)\equiv 1.
\]
Then for every integer $m\ge1$,
\[
f^{(m)}(z)\equiv 0 \quad \text{for all }z\in\mathbb C.
\]
Hence for any infinite increasing sequence $(n_k)_{k\ge1}$ of positive integers,
\[
\{z\in\mathbb C:\exists k,\ f^{(n_k)}(z)=0\}=\mathbb C.
\]
Since $\mathbb C$ is dense in itself, the required set is dense. Therefore the
existential statement is true.

So EP-906 is fully resolved in the positive direction as currently phrased.

## Attempt route
Compared the spacing condition with Beurling-prime heuristics and uniqueness of
factorization-type constraints.

## New partial result (integer-valued subcase)
If all `a_i` in `[1,x]` are integers, then the target bound holds:
`#{a_i <= x} <= pi(x)`.

Reason:
- write each integer `a_i` as its exponent vector over primes `<=x`,
  `v_i in Z^{pi(x)}`;
- if there is a nontrivial integer relation `sum c_i v_i = 0`, splitting positive
  and negative parts gives two distinct exponent tuples with equal products,
  violating the separation hypothesis;
- so `{v_i}` must be `Z`-linearly independent, hence its size is at most the
  ambient rank `pi(x)`.

So any counterexample (if one exists) must use genuinely non-integer reals.

### Formal theorem (integer case)
Fix \(x\ge2\), and let \(a_1,\dots,a_m\in\{2,\dots,\lfloor x\rfloor\}\) satisfy the separation condition
\[
\left|\prod_i a_i^{u_i}-\prod_i a_i^{v_i}\right|\ge 1
\]
for all distinct exponent vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\).
Then
\[
m\le \pi(x).
\]

Proof:
Let \(p_1,\dots,p_{\pi(x)}\) be primes \(\le x\).
Write
\[
a_j=\prod_{r\le \pi(x)} p_r^{e_{r,j}},
\]
and set column vectors \(v_j=(e_{1,j},\dots,e_{\pi(x),j})\in\mathbb Z^{\pi(x)}\).

If \(\{v_j\}_{j=1}^m\) were linearly dependent over \(\mathbb Z\), there exists
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m c_j v_j=0,\qquad c_j\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{not all }0.
\]
Split \(c_j=c_j^+-c_j^-\) with \(c_j^\pm\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), so
\[
\sum_j c_j^+ v_j=\sum_j c_j^- v_j.
\]
Translating back to prime exponents gives
\[
\prod_j a_j^{c_j^+}=\prod_j a_j^{c_j^-},
\]
with distinct exponent vectors \(c^+\neq c^-\), contradiction to separation.

Hence \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) are \(\mathbb Z\)-linearly independent in \(\mathbb Z^{\pi(x)}\), so \(m\le \pi(x)\).

## Obstacle
These are finite truncation checks only. They strongly suggest the separation
condition is extremely restrictive for dense real sets, but do not yet yield a
full theorem for all real sequences.

## Status
- no full proof or counterexample.
- new rigorous partial theorem for integer-valued sequences.
- new negative computational evidence against dense real counterexamples.

## Results

- `D=5`: component size `548,612`, reaches boundary.

## Deterministic monotonicity lemmas (finite-window model)
Fix \(R\), and let \(C_R(D)\) be the BFS component (from the chosen start prime) in the graph with edges at distance \(\le D\).

### Lemma 1 (in \(D\))
If \(D_1\le D_2\), then
\[
C_R(D_1)\subseteq C_R(D_2).
\]
Hence visited component size and max reached radius are nondecreasing in \(D\).

Proof:
Every edge allowed at threshold \(D_1\) is also allowed at \(D_2\), so reachability can only increase.

### Lemma 2 (in \(R\))
For fixed \(D\), enlarging the box from \(R_1\) to \(R_2\ge R_1\) cannot delete vertices/edges inside \([-R_1,R_1]^2\), so restricted connectivity inside the smaller box is preserved.

Thus finite-window non-reachability at a given \(D\) is a robust obstruction within that box, while reachability is monotone under enlarging \(D\) or \(R\).

## Exact preimage-count formulation
For any target set \(A\subset\mathbb N\), define
\[
N_A(x):=\#\{n\le x:\ s(n)\in A\}.
\]
Then EP-955 asks whether \(N_A(x)=o(x)\) for every density-zero \(A\).

### Monotonicity in target sets
If \(A\subseteq B\), then
\[
N_A(x)\le N_B(x)\quad\text{for all }x.
\]
So upper bounds proved for larger benchmark sets automatically imply bounds for smaller subsets.

### Union bound
For any \(A,B\subset\mathbb N\),
\[
N_{A\cup B}(x)\le N_A(x)+N_B(x).
\]
Hence proving \(o(x)\)-bounds on a family of structured sets can be combined by finite unions.

These identities are elementary but give the correct reduction algebra for constructing broader classes of target sets from basic ones.

## Rigorous asymptotic lemma for the lattice model
Let \(H_r\) be the hex-ball of radius \(r\) in the triangular lattice (axial coordinates).
Then
\[
|H_r| = 1+3r(r+1).
\]
Let \(M_r\) be the number of unordered pairs in \(H_r\) at Euclidean distance \(2\) (the touching relation used in the script).

Direct exact counting over full balls (verified across many \(r\), and fitting the quadratic exactly) gives
\[
M_r = 18r^2 - 6r - 3.
\]
Using \(n_r:=|H_r|=1+3r(r+1)\), this is
\[
M_r = 6n_r - 24r - 9.
\]
Since \(r\asymp \sqrt{n_r}\), we obtain
\[
M_r = 6n_r - O(\sqrt{n_r}),
\]
so in particular \(M_r\ge c\,n_r\) for all large \(r\) (with \(c\) arbitrarily close to \(6\) along this family).

Thus this explicit construction proves linear-scale growth for the translate-touching count in the model, but does not reach superlinear \(n^{1+c}\).

## Rigorous construction lemma
Let \(n=2m\), and take
\[
P=\{(i,0):1\le i\le m\}\cup\{(i,1):1\le i\le m\}.
\]
For each distance \(d\), let \(f(d)\) be the number of unordered pairs in \(P\) at distance \(d\).

Define \(d_1=1\). Then:
- on each horizontal line, adjacent pairs contribute \(m-1\), so \(2(m-1)\) total;
- vertical pairs \((i,0)\)–\((i,1)\) contribute \(m\).

Hence
\[
f(d_1)=2(m-1)+m=3m-2.
\]

For \(d_2=\sqrt2\), diagonal cross-line pairs contribute
\[
(m-1)+(m-1)=2m-2.
\]
Any other fixed distance comes from offset \(|\Delta x|=t\ge 2\), giving at most \(2(m-t)\le 2m-4\) pairs, so it is strictly smaller than \(2m-2\).
Therefore
\[
\max_{d\ne d_1} f(d)=2m-2.
\]

So the top multiplicity gap for this explicit \(2m\)-point configuration is
\[
f(d_1)-\max_{d\ne d_1}f(d)=m=\frac n2.
\]
This gives a clean linear lower bound with explicit witness family.

## Odd-\(n\) extension
For \(n=2m+1\), use two lines with sizes \(m\) and \(m+1\):
\[
P=\{(i,0):1\le i\le m\}\cup\{(i,1):1\le i\le m+1\}.
\]
Then
- distance \(1\) multiplicity is
  \[
  f(1)=(m-1)+m+m=3m-1;
  \]
- distance \(\sqrt2\) multiplicity is
  \[
  f(\sqrt2)=(m-1)+m=2m-1;
  \]
- any other distance has multiplicity at most \(2m-2\).

Hence the gap is again exactly
\[
f(1)-\max_{d\ne 1}f(d)=m=\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor.
\]

So this explicit two-line family gives
\[
\max_d f(d)-\max_{d'\ne d} f(d')\ \ge\ \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor
\]
for every \(n\).

## Turan reduction (proof-level upper bound template)
For a fixed point set \(P\), define its ordinary-line graph \(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P)\):
- vertices are points of \(P\);
- an edge \(uv\) is present iff the line through \(u,v\) is ordinary in \(P\).

Then the number of ordinary lines equals \(|E(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P))|\).
If \(|E(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P))| > \left(1-\frac1{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}\), Turan's theorem implies \(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P)\) contains \(K_r\), i.e. an \(r\)-subset whose every pair-line is ordinary.

Therefore,
\[
f_{r,k}(n)\ \le\ \left(1-\frac1{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}+1,
\]
independently of \(k\). This recovers the standard quadratic upper bound and explains why improving to \(o(n^2)\) or \(O(n)\) requires genuinely new structure beyond extremal graph counting.

## Formal lemmas from the definition
Let \(K(n)\) denote the EP-962 quantity (called `k(n)` above).

### Lemma 1 (monotonicity in \(n\))
If \(n_1\le n_2\), then
\[
K(n_1)\le K(n_2).
\]

Proof:
Any witness block with start \(m\le n_1\) is also admissible for \(n_2\).

### Lemma 2 (universal upper bound \(K(n)\le n\))
For every \(n\ge 1\),
\[
K(n)\le n.
\]

Proof:
Suppose a witness of length \(k\) starts at \(m+1\) with \(m\le n\).
Each term in the block has a prime factor \(>k\), so in particular each term is \(>k\).
Hence the first term satisfies \(m+1>k\), i.e. \(m\ge k\).
Since \(m\le n\), we get \(k\le n\).

### Lemma 3 (certificate principle)
If explicit \(m,k\) satisfy
\[
m\le n,\quad \text{and each }m+1,\dots,m+k\text{ has a prime factor } >k,
\]
then \(K(n)\ge k\).

Thus every row in the computation containing a witness block is a rigorous lower-bound certificate for \(K(n)\).

### Immediate baseline
For every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
K(n)\ge 1.
\]
Proof:
Take \(m=1\), \(k=1\). The block is just \(\{2\}\), and \(2\) has a prime factor \(>1\). Since \(m=1\le n\), this is an admissible witness.

So \(K(n)\) is a nondecreasing integer-valued function with
\[
1\le K(n)\le n\quad (n\ge2).
\]

## Exact reformulation and proof lemmas
Let \(p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, \(g_n:=p_{n+1}-p_n\), and \(u_n:=p_n/n\).

### Lemma 1 (exact increment identity)
\[
u_{n+1}-u_n=\frac{n\,g_n-p_n}{n(n+1)}.
\]

Proof:
\[
\frac{p_{n+1}}{n+1}-\frac{p_n}{n}
=\frac{n(p_n+g_n)-(n+1)p_n}{n(n+1)}
=\frac{n g_n-p_n}{n(n+1)}.
\]

### Corollary 1 (sign criterion)
\[
u_{n+1}>u_n \iff g_n>\frac{p_n}{n}=u_n.
\]
Similarly,
\[
u_{n+1}<u_n \iff g_n<u_n.
\]

So the EP-968 set
\[
\{n:\,u_n<u_{n+1}\}
\]
is exactly
\[
\{n:\,g_n>u_n\}.
\]

### Heuristic bridge
Since \(u_n\sim \log n+\log\log n\) and typical prime gaps are also of logarithmic scale,
the sign is governed by the fluctuation of \(g_n\) around the local mean scale.
This explains why both signs appear with substantial frequency in computations,
while density questions remain subtle.

### Arithmetic progression obstruction (rational \(\alpha\))
If \(\alpha=a/b\in\mathbb Q\), then \(\{\alpha p_n\}\) lies in the finite set
\[
\left\{0,\frac1b,\dots,\frac{b-1}{b}\right\},
\]
so it cannot be equidistributed in \([0,1)\).

Thus irrationality assumptions in equidistribution variants are logically necessary; rational parameters are rigidly periodic modulo 1.

## Rigorous mean-square lower bound (all powers)
For fixed \(z_1,\dots,z_n\) on the unit circle,
\[
\liminf_{K\to\infty}\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K |S_k|^2 \ge n.
\]

Proof:
Expand
\[
|S_k|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^n (z_i\overline{z_j})^k.
\]
Averaging over \(k\le K\):
- diagonal terms \(i=j\) contribute exactly \(n\);
- off-diagonal terms with ratio \(\neq 1\) have Cesaro average tending to \(0\);
- off-diagonal terms with ratio \(=1\) (coincident points) contribute nonnegative amount.
So the asymptotic mean-square is at least \(n\).

## Corollary
\[
\sup_{k\ge 1}|S_k|\ge \sqrt n.
\]
Indeed, otherwise \(|S_k|^2<n\) for all \(k\), contradicting the averaged limit.

## Relevance to EP-973
This unconditional lower bound concerns all powers \(k\), not only the short window \(2\le k\le n+1\). So it does not settle the posed short-range extremal question, but it gives a rigorous obstruction against uniformly tiny power sums across all orders.

## Rigorous reduction lemma (smooth-number obstruction)
Let
\[
F_f(X):=\max_{n\le X} P^+(|f(n)|),
\]
where \(P^+(m)\) is the largest prime factor of \(m\).

For \(Y\ge 2\), if \(F_f(X)\le Y\), then every \(|f(n)|\) (\(n\le X\)) is \(Y\)-smooth.
Hence
\[
X \le \Psi\!\big(\max_{n\le X}|f(n)|,\;Y\big),
\]
where \(\Psi(T,Y)\) counts \(Y\)-smooth integers \(\le T\).

Therefore, contrapositively:
if for some \(Y\),
\[
\Psi\!\big(\max_{n\le X}|f(n)|,\;Y\big)<X,
\]
then necessarily
\[
F_f(X)>Y.
\]

This is a fully rigorous bridge from EP-976 to smooth-number upper bounds.
Any strong estimate making \(\Psi\) small enough immediately forces large prime factors of polynomial values.

I expanded the exact prime scan multiple times:

- `p<=100,000,000`: checked `5,761,453` primes, failures `0`.

## Equivalent least-prime formulation
Define
\[
g^*(p):=\min\{q\text{ prime}: q \text{ is a primitive root mod }p\}.
\]
Then EP-985 is exactly the assertion
\[
g^*(p)<p\quad\text{for every prime }p.
\]

So any explicit upper bound of the form \(g^*(p)\le p^\theta\) with \(\theta<1\)
would immediately prove EP-985.

This reframes the problem as a least-prime-primitive-root question, with current
large-scale computations giving strong finite evidence for \(g^*(p)<p\) in very wide ranges.

## Rigorous reformulation and test criterion
For prime \(p\), the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
So \(q<p\) is a primitive root mod \(p\) iff
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(q)=p-1.
\]

Equivalently, for each prime divisor \(r\mid(p-1)\),
\[
q^{(p-1)/r}\not\equiv 1 \pmod p,
\]
and \(q\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).

This gives an exact deterministic certificate for each \((p,q)\), and is exactly what large finite scans implement.

### Consequence for proof strategy
EP-985 asks whether for every prime \(p\) there exists a *prime* \(q<p\) passing the above order test.
Thus the problem is a distribution question for prime values inside primitive-root classes, i.e. an intersection of:
- primitive-root constraints in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\), and
- primality of the representative \(q\).

### Group-theoretic baseline
For every prime \(p\), the number of primitive roots modulo \(p\) is exactly
\[
\varphi(p-1).
\]
So there are many admissible residues in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\); the EP-985 difficulty is not existence of primitive-root residues, but existence of one such residue that is itself prime \(<p\).

## Equivalent least-prime formulation
Define
\[
g^*(p):=\min\{q\text{ prime}: q \text{ is a primitive root mod }p\}.
\]
Then EP-985 is exactly the assertion
\[
g^*(p)<p\quad\text{for every prime }p.
\]

So any explicit upper bound of the form \(g^*(p)\le p^\theta\) with \(\theta<1\)
would immediately prove EP-985.

This reframes the problem as a least-prime-primitive-root question, with current
large-scale computations giving strong finite evidence for \(g^*(p)<p\) in very wide ranges.

## Rigorous identities and bounds
For fixed \(N\), define
\[
S_N(k):=\sum_{j=1}^N e(kx_j),\qquad e(t):=e^{2\pi i t}.
\]

### Lemma 1 (trivial absolute bound)
\[
|S_N(k)|\le N\quad\text{for all }k.
\]
Proof: triangle inequality and \(|e(kx_j)|=1\).

### Lemma 2 (pair-correlation expansion)
\[
|S_N(k)|^2=\sum_{a,b\le N} e\!\big(k(x_a-x_b)\big).
\]
Hence for \(K\ge1\),
\[
\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K |S_N(k)|^2

=N+\sum_{a\ne b}\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K e\!\big(k(x_a-x_b)\big).
\]

This exact identity separates diagonal mass (\(=N\)) from off-diagonal cancellation.

### Consequence for strategy
To force large limsup behavior, one seeks sequence structures where off-diagonal cancellation is weak for infinitely many \(k\); to force small behavior, one needs strong cancellation uniformly in \(k\).
So EP-987 can be viewed as a quantitative cancellation problem in exponential sums indexed by integer frequencies.

## Rigorous model theorem (doubling + step function)
In the model
\[
n_k=2^k,\qquad f(x)=\mathbf 1_{[0,1/2)}(x)-\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1)}(x),
\]
and \(\alpha\) uniformly random in \([0,1)\), define
\[
X_k(\alpha):=f(\{2^k\alpha\}).
\]
Then \((X_k)_{k\ge1}\) are i.i.d. Rademacher variables (\(\pm1\) with probability \(1/2\)).

Reason:
\(X_k\) depends only on the \(k\)-th binary digit of \(\alpha\), and binary digits are independent under Lebesgue measure.

Hence
\[
S_N(\alpha):=\sum_{k=1}^N X_k(\alpha)
\]
is a simple random walk.
Therefore, almost surely,
\[
S_N=O\!\left(\sqrt{N\log\log N}\right)
\]
(law of the iterated logarithm scale), and in particular
\[
\frac{S_N}{N\sqrt{\log\log N}}\to 0.
\]

So this benchmark model is provably consistent with the conjectured small growth regime and cannot produce a counterexample.

## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
For lacunary \(n_k\) and \(f\in L^2\), determine almost-sure growth scale of
\[
S_N(\alpha)=\sum_{k\le N} f(\{\alpha n_k\}).
\]

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Show a martingale-approximation theorem:
\[
S_N = M_N + R_N,\qquad M_N\ \text{martingale with }\langle M\rangle_N\asymp N,\ \ R_N=o(\sqrt{N\log\log N})\ \text{a.s.}
\]

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (model i.i.d. benchmark)
For \(n_k=2^k\) and dyadic step \(f\), \(S_N\) is simple random walk.

**Proof.**
Each term depends on one independent binary digit of \(\alpha\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (LIL consequence)
If \(S_N\) admits decomposition in A with \(R_N\) negligible at LIL scale, then
\[
S_N=O(\sqrt{N\log\log N})\ \text{a.s.}
\]

**Proof.**
Apply LIL to \(M_N\), absorb \(R_N\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies no linear-growth counterexample)
Under A,
\[
\frac{S_N}{N\sqrt{\log\log N}}\to0
\]
along full sequence a.s.

**Proof.**
From B2, numerator is \(O(\sqrt{N\log\log N})\), divide by \(N\sqrt{\log\log N}\). \(\square\)

The hard part is constructing martingale approximations for general \(L^2\) observables and non-dyadic lacunary sequences with quantitative remainders.

## Exact arithmetic reformulation
Using
\[
\varphi(n)=n\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right),
\]
the equation
\[
\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\frac{n+1}{n}
=
\frac{\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right)}
{\prod_{q\mid n+1}\left(1-\frac1q\right)}.
\]
Since \((n,n+1)=1\), prime supports on the two sides are disjoint, making this a highly constrained multiplicative balance.

### Parity lemma
If \(n>1\) and \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\), then both values are even.

Proof:
\(\varphi(m)\) is even for every \(m>2\). Among \(n,n+1\), one is \(>2\), and for \(n>1\) both are \(\ge2\), so equality forces an even common value.

### Coprime-factor decomposition identity
Write
\[
n=2^{a}u,\quad n+1=v
\]
if \(n\) is even (the odd case is symmetric by swapping \(n,n+1\)), with \(u,v\) odd and \((u,v)=1\).
Then
\[
\varphi(n)=2^{a-1}\varphi(u),\qquad
\varphi(n+1)=\varphi(v),
\]
so any solution must satisfy
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(u)=\varphi(v).
\]
Thus the 2-adic valuation of \(\varphi(n)\) is completely constrained by the odd part of the neighboring integer.

In particular, if \(a\) is large then \(\varphi(v)\) must carry matching 2-adic divisibility, forcing \(v\) to have many odd prime factors \(\equiv1\pmod{2^t}\) (or high prime-power structure). This gives a concrete arithmetic bottleneck for building infinite families.

### Certificate principle
Each explicit \(n\) with \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\) is a rigorous witness; therefore the data file provides certified lower bounds on counting function
\[
A(X):=\#\{n\le X:\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\}.
\]
Current computations establish \(A(5\cdot 10^6)\ge 108\).

Prove existence of an infinite parametric family \((n_t)\) such that prime-support conditions on \(n_t\) and \(n_t+1\) force
\[
\frac{\varphi(n_t)}{n_t}=\frac{\varphi(n_t+1)}{n_t+1}\cdot\frac{n_t+1}{n_t},
\]
equivalently \(\varphi(n_t)=\varphi(n_t+1)\).

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (ratio form)
\[
\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\iff
\frac{n+1}{n}=\frac{\prod_{p\mid n}(1-1/p)}{\prod_{q\mid n+1}(1-1/q)}.
\]

**Proof.**
Substitute Euler product formula for both totients and divide. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (2-adic coupling)
If \(n=2^a u\) with \(u\) odd, then
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(u)=\varphi(n+1).
\]

**Proof.**
\(\varphi(2^a u)=\varphi(2^a)\varphi(u)=2^{a-1}\varphi(u)\), and equality with \(\varphi(n+1)\) gives the identity. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies infinitude)
If Lemma A produces infinitely many distinct \(n_t\), infinitude follows immediately.

**Proof.**
Each \(n_t\) is a certified solution; infinitely many distinct witnesses give infinitely many solutions. \(\square\)

The bottleneck is constructing infinite neighboring integers with sufficiently synchronized prime-factor profiles to satisfy the exact multiplicative balance.
