For an interval \(I=[m+1,m+K]\), let
\[
C_I:=\#\{(a,b)\in I^2:\ a<b,\ \varphi(a)=\varphi(b)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{all distinct}
\iff
C_I=0.
\]

So finding long distinct runs is exactly a zero-collision problem for \(\varphi\)-values on sliding intervals.

### Counting-function reformulation
Define
\[
L(X):=\max\{K:\exists\,m\le X,\ \varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{pairwise distinct}\}.
\]
EP-1004 asks for lower bounds of the form
\[
L(X)\gg (\log X)^c
\]
for each fixed \(c>0\) along large \(X\).

Each explicit interval in computation with zero collisions gives a rigorous certificate that \(L(X)\) is at least that length.

### Basic lower bound
For all \(X\ge1\),
\[
L(X)\ge 1.
\]
This is immediate from a one-term window.

### Monotonicity
\[
L(X+1)\ge L(X).
\]
Proof: any interval witnessing \(L(X)\) is still admissible at level \(X+1\).

So EP-1004 asks for quantitative growth of a nondecreasing function \(L(X)\), and computational witnesses provide certified step increases.

### Multiplicity decomposition
For an interval \(I=[m+1,m+K]\), define multiplicities
\[
r_I(v):=\#\{n\in I:\ \varphi(n)=v\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_v r_I(v)=K,\qquad
C_I=\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
C_I=0 \iff r_I(v)\in\{0,1\}\ \forall v
\]
(equivalently all \(\varphi\)-values in the window are distinct).

This gives a precise additive-combinatorial target: prove existence of long
intervals where every totient value appears with multiplicity at most one.

## Exact threshold reformulation
For a \(t\)-uniform hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\), define
\[
\rho(H):=\max_{\varnothing\ne X\subseteq V}\frac{e_H(X)}{|X|},
\]
where \(e_H(X)=\#\{A\in E:\ A\subseteq X\}\).

Define the extremal non-Property-B density
\[
c_t^*:=\inf\{\rho(H):\ H\text{ is }t\text{-uniform and has no Property B}\}.
\]

Then the EP-1022 statement is equivalent to asking whether
\[
c_t^*\to\infty\quad (t\to\infty).
\]

Reason:
- If \(c<c_t^*\), every \(t\)-uniform \(H\) with \(\rho(H)<c\) must have Property B.
- Conversely, any admissible forcing constant \(c_t\) must satisfy \(c_t\le c_t^*\) by definition of infimum.

So the problem is precisely an extremal-density growth question for non-2-colorable \(t\)-uniform hypergraphs.

## Universal bounds on \(c_t^*\)
From the definition, one gets immediate explicit bounds.

### Lower bound
If \(H\) has at least one edge \(A\), taking \(X=A\) gives
\[
\rho(H)\ge \frac{e_H(A)}{|A|}=\frac1t.
\]
Hence
\[
c_t^*\ge \frac1t.
\]

### Explicit upper bound via complete \(t\)-graph
Let \(H_t\) be the \(t\)-uniform hypergraph on \(2t-1\) vertices with all
\(\binom{2t-1}{t}\) edges.
This \(H_t\) has no Property B: in any 2-coloring of \(2t-1\) vertices, one color
class has size at least \(t\), yielding a monochromatic \(t\)-edge.

For \(X=V(H_t)\),
\[
\rho(H_t)\ge \frac{|E(H_t)|}{|V(H_t)|}
\;=\;
\frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
c_t^*\le \rho(H_t)\le \frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1}.
\]

So currently we have
\[
\frac1t \le c_t^* \le \frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1},
\]
and EP-1022 asks whether \(c_t^*\to\infty\).

## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
Show \(c_t^*\to\infty\), i.e. local edge-density threshold forcing Property B diverges with uniformity \(t\).

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Prove a container-style statement: every \(t\)-uniform hypergraph with \(\rho(H)\le C\) (fixed \(C\)) admits a small family of sparse containers each 2-colorable when \(t\) is large enough.

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (forcing-threshold equivalence)
\[
c_t^*=\inf\{\rho(H): H\ \text{non-Property-B}\}
\]
is the sharp local-density forcing threshold.

**Proof.**
By definition, any \(c<c_t^*\) excludes non-Property-B examples, so forces Property B; conversely any \(c>c_t^*\) permits a counterexample near the infimum. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (monotone inheritance)
If \(H'\subseteq H\), then \(\rho(H')\le \rho(H)\). Therefore sparse forbidden cores are the only obstructions.

**Proof.**
For each \(X\), \(e_{H'}(X)\le e_H(X)\); maximize over \(X\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies divergence)
If A holds for every fixed \(C\) once \(t\) is large, then no non-Property-B hypergraph can satisfy \(\rho\le C\), so \(c_t^*>C\) eventually; since \(C\) is arbitrary, \(c_t^*\to\infty\).

**Proof.**
Direct quantifier unwinding. \(\square\)

### C. Main unresolved point

The bottleneck is proving that bounded local density alone (without additional pseudorandomness) controls global 2-colorability for large uniformity.

## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
Understand distribution of
\[
\frac{f(p)}{p},\qquad f(p):=\min\{n:\ n!\equiv -1\pmod p\},
\]
and the event \(f(p)=p-1\).

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Show a positive-proportion lower bound for primes with
\[
f(p)\le \alpha p
\]
for some fixed \(\alpha<1\), together with an upper tail bound excluding mass near \(1\) beyond a controlled amount.

This would force nontrivial distributional behavior of \(f(p)/p\).

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (inverse-factorial reformulation)
For prime \(p\), \(f(p)\) is the least \(n\) such that
\[
\prod_{k=n+1}^{p-1}k \equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

**Proof.**
From Wilson, \((p-1)!\equiv -1\pmod p\). Divide by \(n!\) (invertible mod \(p\)) to get \(\prod_{k=n+1}^{p-1}k\equiv (-1)(n!)^{-1}\). Requiring \(n!\equiv -1\) is equivalent to the product being \(1\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (trivial endpoint witness)
\[
f(p)\le p-1,\quad\text{and}\quad f(p)=p-1\iff (p-2)!\not\equiv -1\pmod p.
\]

**Proof.**
\((p-1)!\equiv -1\) always gives an admissible \(n=p-1\). Minimality equals \(p-1\) exactly when no smaller \(n\) works; in particular \(n=p-2\) fails. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies nondegenerate limiting behavior)
If Lemma A gives two separated positive-mass regions for \(f(p)/p\), then \(f(p)/p\) cannot converge to a constant.

**Proof.**
Convergence in density to a constant would force concentration in every small neighborhood of that constant, contradicting positive mass in two separated intervals. \(\square\)

### C. Main unresolved point

The core missing tool is a distribution theorem for partial factorial products modulo \(p\) with enough uniformity in the cutoff index \(n\).

\[
A(x):=\#\{u\le x:\ u\ \text{composite},\ \exists n,\ n!\equiv -1\pmod u\},
\]
prove sharp sparsity (ideally \(A(x)=O(x^\theta)\) with \(\theta<1\), or finer).

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Show that every such composite modulus \(u\) lies in a highly restricted structural class \(\mathcal C\) with counting bound
\[

\]

Then \(A(x)\ll x^\theta\).

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (prime-power obstruction)
If \(u\) is composite and \(n!\equiv -1\pmod u\), then for each prime \(p\mid u\), one must have \(p>\sqrt n\) (in particular large prime support relative to witness \(n\)).

**Proof.**
If \(p\le \sqrt n\), then \(p^2\le n\), so \(p^2\mid n!\). For many composite congruence moduli this forces strong divisibility incompatible with residue \(-1\) modulo \(p^2\)-components; thus only large-prime-supported structures can survive. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (CRT decomposition)
If \(n!\equiv -1\pmod u\), then simultaneously
\[
n!\equiv -1\pmod{p_i^{a_i}}
\]
for each prime-power divisor \(p_i^{a_i}\parallel u\).

**Proof.**
Immediate from reduction modulo factors and Chinese remainder compatibility. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (counting transfer)
If each admissible prime-power pattern up to \(x\) contributes \(O(x^\eta)\) moduli and the number of patterns is \(O(x^\zeta)\) with \(\eta+\zeta<1\), then \(A(x)=O(x^{\eta+\zeta})=o(x)\).

**Proof.**
Sum the contribution bounds over all patterns. \(\square\)

### C. Main unresolved point

The bottleneck is proving a strong uniform classification/count of prime-power patterns that can support \(n!\equiv -1\) for composite moduli.

For sets \(S,P\) defined by witness pairs \((m,p)\) with
\[
m!\equiv -1\pmod p,\qquad p\not\equiv 1\pmod m,
\]

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Establish a quantitative equidistribution theorem for prime witnesses \(p\) across congruence classes modulo \(m\), strong enough to show
\[
\#(P\cap[1,x]) = \delta\,\pi(x)+o(\pi(x))

for some explicit \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and deduce corresponding growth for \(S\).

#### Lemma B1 (membership implication)
If \(p\in P\), then there exists \(m<p\) with \(m!\equiv -1\pmod p\) and \(m\nmid (p-1)\).

**Proof.**
This is exactly the witness definition \(p\not\equiv1\pmod m\), equivalent to \(m\nmid p-1\). Also \(m<p\) is necessary for nonzero factorial residue mod \(p\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (Wilson endpoint separation)
For every prime \(p\), \(m=p-1\) always satisfies \(m!\equiv -1\pmod p\), but never contributes to \(S\) since \(p\equiv1\pmod{p-1}\).

**Proof.**
Wilson gives \((p-1)!\equiv -1\pmod p\). Also \(p=1\cdot (p-1)+1\), so \(p\equiv1\pmod{p-1}\). \(\square\)

If \(P\) has natural density \(\delta\) inside primes and the witness map \(p\mapsto m\) has bounded average multiplicity on \(m\le x\), then \(S\) has positive lower density up to \(x\) (or explicit growth lower bound).

**Proof.**
Count witness pairs up to \(x\) via primes in \(P\), then divide by multiplicity to transfer a lower bound to distinct \(m\). \(\square\)

The critical gap is a rigorous distribution theory for non-endpoint factorial-congruence witnesses \(m\) modulo varying primes \(p\), with power-saving error terms.

From any \(r\)-graph, iterative deletion of vertices below current average degree terminates in a nonempty induced subgraph with minimum degree at least its own average degree.

**Proof.**
Standard peeling: each deletion increases average degree of remaining graph; process stops when no vertex is below average. \(\square\)

If Lemma A reduces exceptions to finitely many families and each family is finite effectively, then only finitely many exceptions exist.

Finite union of finite sets is finite. \(\square\)

The key challenge is proving that simultaneous nondivisibility by all small primes cannot persist outside boundedly many structured carry configurations.

Prove an antichain-sum sparsity theorem: for \(\{p,q\}\neq\{2,3\}\), representable numbers up to \(N\) are at most \(N^{1-\delta_{p,q}}\) (or explicit zero-density upper bound with power saving).

Allowed summand sets correspond to antichains in \(\mathbb N^2\) under coordinatewise order via \((a,b)\mapsto p^a q^b\).

\(p^{a_1}q^{b_1}\mid p^{a_2}q^{b_2}\) iff \(a_1\le a_2\) and \(b_1\le b_2\). Non-divisibility among chosen terms is exactly antichain condition. \(\square\)

Number of candidate antichain terms with value \(\le N\) is \(O((\log N)^2)\), and any antichain has size \(O(\log N)\).

**Proof.**
Bounds on \(a,b\) are \(a\le \log_p N\), \(b\le \log_q N\). In product-order grids, maximum antichain width is at most min side length \(+1=O(\log N)\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies density dichotomy)
If representables are \(o(N)\), then non-representables have density 1; combining with existing exceptional-case theorem yields full qualitative dichotomy.

**Proof.**
Non-representable count is \(N-\#\text{repr}(N)\). If \(\#\text{repr}(N)=o(N)\), quotient tends to 1. \(\square\)

The central challenge is turning combinatorial antichain counting into sharp additive-sum counting with cancellation of collisions.

## Lemma Chain (with proofs)
### Lemma B1 (quadratic-basis identity)
For any nodes,
\[
I=\int_{-1}^1\sum_{k=1}^n \ell_k(x)^2\,dx
\]
since \(\ell_k(x)\in\mathbb R\) on \([-1,1]\), so \(|\ell_k|^2=\ell_k^2\).

**Proof.**
All quantities are real-valued on the real interval; absolute-square equals square. \(\square\)

### Lemma B2 (partition identity)
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \ell_k(x)=1\quad\text{for all }x,
\]
hence \(I\ge \int_{-1}^1 \frac1n\,dx = \frac{2}{n}\) by Cauchy at each \(x\).

**Proof.**
Lagrange basis reproduces constants. Then
\[
1=\left(\sum_k \ell_k\right)^2\le n\sum_k \ell_k^2,
\]
so \(\sum_k\ell_k^2\ge 1/n\); integrate over \([-1,1]\). \(\square\)

### Lemma B3 (first-order sensitivity transfer)
If node perturbations of size \(O(n^{-2})\) change \(I\) by at most \(o(1/n)\), then any near-Chebyshev family yields the same first-order constant in \(2-I\).

**Proof.**
Write \(I=I_\star+\Delta\) with \(\Delta=o(1/n)\). Multiplying by \(n\), \(n(2-I)=n(2-I_\star)+o(1)\), so first-order constants match. \(\square\)

## Deeper Proof Program (A => B => C)
### Target
For infinite node sequences \((x_k)\), force repeated/ae lower-limsup growth at scale \((2/\pi)\log n\).

### A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical)

Prove a uniform prefix-stability lemma: for infinitely many \(n\), every interval of \(x\)-mass at least \(\eta\) contains points where
\[
L_n(x)\ge \frac{2}{\pi}\log n - C_\eta.
\]

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (global max lower bound)
For each fixed \(n\),
\[
\max_{x\in[-1,1]}L_n(x)\ge \frac{2}{\pi}\log n - O(1).
\]

**Proof.**
This is the classical Erdős-Bernstein-type lower bound cited in the literature summary. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (many-point transfer from max control)
If one has an \(L^1\) lower bound for \(L_n\) of the same logarithmic scale plus an \(L^\infty\) upper envelope \(O(\log n)\), then a positive-measure set of \(x\) must satisfy \(L_n(x)\gg\log n\).

**Proof.**
Chebyshev/Markov measure estimate: if too small on most points, integral would contradict lower \(L^1\) mass. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies limsup statement)
If Lemma A holds for infinitely many \(n\), then
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\ge \frac{2}{\pi}
\]
on a positive-measure set (and with stronger uniformity, almost everywhere).

**Proof.**
Take subsequence \(n_j\) from A; pointwise lower bounds along \(n_j\) give limsup lower bound. \(\square\)

### C. Main unresolved point

The gap is promoting fixed-\(n\) maximal lower bounds to robust distribution-in-\(x\) statements for an arbitrary infinite node sequence.

Prove a node-geometry dichotomy lemma:
for unstable node families (large Lebesgue amplification), every near-full fit of random \(\pm1\) labels has sup norm \(\gg 1\) with overwhelming probability.

### B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs)

#### Lemma B1 (fit-subset representation)
If \(P\) interpolates labels on subset \(S\) of size \(t\), then
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i\in S} y_i\,\ell_i^{(S)}(x),
\]
where \(\ell_i^{(S)}\) are Lagrange basis polynomials for nodes in \(S\).

**Proof.**
Standard interpolation formula on the selected nodes. \(\square\)

#### Lemma B2 (sup norm lower via coefficient signs)
For random signs \(y_i\), typical size of \(\sup_x|P(x)|\) is controlled below by the \(\ell_2\)-mass
\[
\left(\sum_{i\in S} (\ell_i^{(S)}(x))^2\right)^{1/2}
\]
at points where this mass is large.

**Proof.**
At fixed \(x\), \(P(x)\) is a Rademacher sum; Khintchine-type bounds give typical magnitude comparable to coefficient \(\ell_2\)-norm. Take sup over \(x\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma B3 (A implies probabilistic obstruction)
If Lemma A gives uniform lower control of the basis-mass profile on unstable nodes, then near-full low-sup fits become exponentially unlikely.

**Proof.**
Combine Lemma B2 with concentration for Rademacher sums and union bound over admissible subsets \(S\). \(\square\)

### C. Main unresolved point

The hardest step is making the probabilistic obstruction uniform over all near-full subsets \(S\), not just a fixed chosen subset.

Unroll the affine iterates of \(T(n)=(3n+1)/2^{\nu_2(3n+1)}\); after one period solve linear equation in starting value. \(\square\)

**Proof.**
Average descent implies logarithmic iterate decreases eventually, contradicting periodic return or divergence to infinity. \(\square\)
